items.title: All the Worst Government GTA Memes from Around the World
items.author: Matthew Gault
items.content:
is a true . Every news channel is covering it, anyone with a passing interest in video games is playing it, and it’s in less than a week. Desperate to connect with constituents, governments around the world have tried to capitalize on GTA’s popularity by releasing some of the worst AI-generated memes I’ve ever seen. The pictures of politicians in the hyper-real cartoon pink-tinted style of GTA 6 are so awful they even caused a minor political scandal in Scotland.

Let’s begin in the United States, where Vice President JD Vance, the White House, and several other government-run X accounts attempted to capture the cultural zeitgeist by quickly churning out AI-generated meme garbage. GTA has long been popular with Trump 2.0 officials. In March, the official X account of the White House published a compilation of strikes on Iranian targets overlaid with the “WASTED” game over screen from GTA. 

In one of the more embarrassing exchanges, the X account for House Republicans posted an AI-generated picture of Hakeem Jefferies, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Abdul El-Sayed above the words “Grand Theft Taxpayer.” A Democrat-linked account then replied with its own picture of Trump and the words “Grand Theft Autocrat.” Embarrassing for all involved.

Israel also got in on the action. On the Friday after the game’s release, U.S. ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee shared a “Shabbot Shalom” meme in the GTA style. The Israel Defense Force’s Farsi X account posted several pictures of dead Iranian officials captioned as “WASTED.”

“We saw all this killing before GTA6,” the post said in Persian, referring to the now retired meme we got something before GTA 6. This account posts in Farsi and meant for “direct dialogue between us and you,” meaning Israel and Iran, according to its bio on X.

In India, Prime Minister Narenda Modi and his Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) posted GTA memes repeatedly on November 19, the day the game was released.

Indian politician and frequent Modi critic Jairam Ramesh mocked Modi for the posts on social media. “The PM in a desperate bid to reach out to the youth has resorted to GTA V and GTA VI imagery on social media,” Ramesh . “Recall that this video game follows a criminal duo. How very appropriate.”

On Instagram, Singapore’s Land Transport Authority made fun of people who can’t navigate the country’s rail system. “If he can memorize the entire GTA6 map, he can memorize the Singapore MRT System Map,” . “Bro knows every corner of Leonida but still saves the SG MRT System Map on his phone to get to Orchard. 💀”

NATO posted its attempt at being part of the cultural conversation on Instagram. “Wanted level: NATO,” the post said above the pink-hued cross cut collage of military images in the GTA style. “The final boss of wanted levels. Think you could fend off the most successful Alliance in history? NATO isn’t part of GTA6 of course, but if it was, we think even the best gamers would have a challenge with this one.”

In Scotland, the Scottish National Party (SNP) posted GTA 6 memes so cringe that they talked about it on the floor of parliament. On November 19, the SNP social media accounts posted AI-generated pictures of Boris Johnson and Margaret Thatcher in the GTA style. “When the loading screen so long you start seeing characters you’ve never seen before,” one image said over a picture of Thatcher pouring a bag of “Scottish oil money” into the UK treasury.

Scotland’s Green Party didn’t find the memes funny. Rockstar is originally Scottish, was founded in Edinburgh, and still maintains a significant studio there. In parliament, Green co-leader Gillian Mackay said she was proud of what all of Rockstar’s workers had done to stand up against bad working conditions and produce a work of art like GTA 6. Then she made comments about SNP leader and Scottish First Minister John Swiney. 

“Last night the SNP angered anti-AI campaigners by posting AI-generated GTA memes on its social media despite huge concerns about the impact of AI and AI data centers on artists, workers, and the environment,” Mackay said in the parliament . “Does the first minister understand why people are concerned about his government’s approach to AI and the big companies behind it.”

The SNP deleted the memes and Swiney apologized. “First of all, let me say that I don’t want to offend anyone by anything that we get up to, so if I’ve offended anyone about that, I’m sorry about that. It was not my intention,” Swiney said in the Scottish parliament. Then he said he shared concerns about AI but defended the technology’s use for healthcare.

There will be more bad posts like this. hasn’t been out for even a week and the memetic landscape around it will shift and change. We don’t even know what the dominant memes for the game are yet, let alone the innovative ways posters will iterate on them. Rest assured, however, that the governments of the world are watching and waiting to post their own variations and make it all cringe.

items.title: Pass the Controller: How Single Console Households Split 'GTA VI'
items.author: Megan Farokhmanesh
items.content:
is 2026’s breakout entertainment event. By the numbers, it made roughly $3.79 billion in revenue at launch, outpacing the lifetime earnings for megahit films like , , and . PlayStation called it their biggest launch of all time with over 39 million players on the platform alone. It’s the center of the current cultural zeitgeist, whether it’s because of the game’s , , , , or its .

Entire households are playing GTA VI with one slight hitch: unlike movies, TV shows, or even books you can read side by side, a single-player, 40+ hour experience is tough to enjoy when you live together. 

For some couples, the solution has been using more than one console or even multiple copies of the game. Married couple Meagan Kelley and Kyle Prahl typically switch between playing different games in the same room, or the same platforms in different parts of the house. The two are parents who find time to game after putting their son to bed. “The nice thing about having really young kids is they do go to bed super early,” Kelley told me. “Usually [my son] goes down and is asleep before eight, so then that's kind of like our prime gaming time.” The couple often plays different games in the same room, but for GTA VI “we're playing separately, so that kind of sucks because it's like we don't get a lot of time for each other,” Kelley said. 

Although some men online have whined about central romance, complaining about doing favors for their in-game girlfriend Lucia (“cuck simulator” being one common refrain), Kelley says the benefits to her real-life relationship are only positive. “It's funny that there's so much online discourse about GTA splitting up relationships and stuff when it's like something that can bring Kyle and I closer,” Kelley said. “Especially as we become parents and need to have more perspective on making sure that we're making time for ourselves.” 

Dividing up time to play and sharing their experiences, she said, adds a new dimension to their mutual hobby. “When we are together taking care of our kid or having conversations, it's almost like book club,” Kelley said. “We share the different ways that we're experiencing the game with choices and stuff like that.” 

Justin Massongill, another GTA VI player, and his wife recently had their second child. “She's taken on a lot,” he said. He bought the game for her, giving her priority to play so she could de-stress.

Massongill watched his wife play the first hour of the game; the next morning, he started his own. “We're kind of trying not to look too much at the other player's screen,” he said. “I don't want to, you know, get spoiled on things. But it's also such a massive game that what are the chances that we're going to see the same thing in the first place?”

Madeline Blondeau and her fiancée decided to buy their copy of together. The $80 price tag wasn’t so bad between the two of them; they downloaded the game, knowing that even with a PlayStation 5 and a PlayStation 5 Pro, they’d have to divvy up time between their single copy. 

“We have been alternating our schedules,” Blondeau said. Her fiancée wakes up at 5 a.m. to start her IT job. Blondeau’s shift starts around 10 a.m. “We've sort of worked this out—me playing while she is working, and then her playing while I am finishing up my shift, trying to tiptoe around spoilers.” 

Even as a queer couple, there’s an equality and care for each other in the experience Blondeau finds reassuring. “I think there's these very gendered expectations in relationships in terms of who games, who is the gamer of the household,” Blondeau said. You even see it in , she adds, where Jason, the game’s male protagonist, will be the one with a controller in his hand. “Breaking down the gendered expectations of who is the gamer in the relationship really opens up a whole avenue for not getting into fights with your partner over video games,” Blondeau said. 

“It feels like two people who figure their shit out, working out equitable time to experience something they've liked their whole lives, and talk about it.”

This past weekend, Blondeau’s fiancé left to grab groceries. She came back with something extra: the trilogy for Nintendo Switch, a consolation prize for whoever wasn’t playing their shared copy of GTA VI. “I was in the mood to play Vice City,” her partner said. “We can trade off."

items.title: Physicists Send an Unblockable Message Using Gravity
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Longtime Slashdot reader fahrbot-bot shares a report from Phys.org: University of Queensland researchers have used gravity to transmit a message through a brick wall using an elevator and a sensitive gravimeter. The unusual experiment took place in UQ's Parnell Building, where the team of physicists sent the elevator back and forth between two levels, moving its 1.8 metric ton (4,000 pound) counterweight between positions representing binary 0 and 1. A gravimeter in an adjacent bathroom detected the changes in the gravitational field and translated the message into a single word, "Gravity." The research has been published in Science Advances.
 
"Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path," [said Dr. Charles Woffinden from the School of Mathematics and Physics]. "While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block." Professor Andrew White said the biggest limitation to future gravity-based communication was its slow speed. "Our elevator was snail-paced -- it's from the 1950s -- so our experiment transmitted just 1 bit per minute, meaning it took an hour to send a single word," White said.
 
"The speed of gravity communication would come down to how big the mass is, how fast you can move it and the sensitivity of the detector. Our experiment used a classical gravity sensor, but our modeling indicates that quantum sensors could, with rather ambitious assumptions, support ranges of up to about 500 meters (1,640 feet) and data rates of around 15 bits per minute."

The e-commerce and cloud computing giant is building a competitor to SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, and said it would take SpaceX "centuries" to build the constellation, adding that the company provided scant details about how it would "deliver on these grand claims." The petition resulted in a rebuke from [FCC Chairman Brendan Carr], who said Amazon "should focus on the fact" that it's falling short of its own satellite deployment milestone. In a post on X, Carr said SpaceX's Starmind constellation and "competitor constellations will use solar power to extend America's lead in Super Intelligence."
 
Musk said in a reply, "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."

items.title: GTA 6 Streams Hit With Takedowns Over In-Game Reggaeton Song
items.author: Timothy Geigner
items.content:
Unless you’re a monk on retreat somewhere, you know that was released in recent days and that roughly the entire world is playing it. And, importantly, putting clips of the game online, or featuring it in let’s play game streams. I haven’t played this thing yet, but I am enjoying the clips. My personal favorites are the ones where the player goes around and randomly throws a basketball at people’s faces. Gets me right in the id.

Now, Rockstar Games has not been shy about DMCAing the shit out of anything it doesn’t like when it comes to its games. The company tries to DMCA leaks out of existence, which never works. It’s also happy to takedown mods for previewing future game content in them and the like. But a recent spate of stream takedowns apparently had nothing to do with Rockstar and might have been YouTube’s Content ID automatic system.

On Nov. 22, streamers who uploaded their GTA 6 gameplay on YouTube were suddenly hit with a barrage of copyright strikes. They all came from a single source: Colombian reggaeton artist Frank “El Santo.” The Medellín-born singer and songwriter, whose real name is Andrés Mauricio Arango Flórez, played GTA 6 on stream on his YouTube channel. His footage was then used to auto-claim copyright on anyone who was playing the game live on YouTube. This resulted in indiscriminate strikes against users, including big channels such as theRadBrad (14.1 million subscribers) and HollowPoiint (5.2 million subscribers).

This seemingly absurd situation arose from a combination of specific circumstances and YouTube’s often-criticized copyright policies. Frank El Santo’s YouTube channel contains his official music videos, so it’s possible that the platform mistakenly deemed the GTA 6 gameplay video eligible for copyright claims. After commenters pointed out the issue during his stream, Arango Flórez deleted the gameplay video, but the copyright strikes continued until the YouTube team intervened.

Now, there’s been some speculation out in the wild that Arango Florez might still have taken some action that resulted in Content ID going kazoo with the takedowns. He insists otherwise. Ultimately, it doesn’t matter all that much, because the real point here is that YouTube’s takedown system remains so absolutely wide open to error, fraud, and abuse that content that pretty much nobody thinks should be taken down gets taken down anyway across a wide swath of targets.

Regardless of the intent, this episode highlights that YouTube’s copyright policies are either ineffective or outright damaging to its users. The company relies on automated processes and AI-assisted tools to detect copyright infringement​​​​​​​, often resulting in videos being taken down or demonetized without proper reason. As HollowPoiint put it in a post on X where he praised YouTube’s quick intervention to resolve the GTA 6 El Santo issue, “Now we just need a better system in place.”

This isn’t a revelation. We’ve been saying this . YouTube’s automatic system has been responsible for a legion of bad takedowns, some of them so absurd it boggles the mind. In the exact moment when Rockstar should, and probably does, want as much of this user hype content out there as possible, some combination of this artist and YouTube got a bunch of streams taken down.

It’s well past time this was fixed. YouTube… what are you waiting for?

items.title: World Has Six Consecutive Days 2C Above Preindustrial Levels For First Time
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Longtime Slashdot reader AmiMoJo shares a report from The Guardian: For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, the Guardian has learned. This record hot streak, which is continuing, is too brief to signify that the upper range of the Paris climate agreement target has been breached, but scientists said it was an early indication of what is to come unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated. It is also likely to feed into growing scientific concerns that global heating may be accelerating. The daily global surface temperature rose to its highest ever point above preindustrial levels, 2.24C, on Monday, the most recent day for which data is available, and is forecast to persist at similarly high levels for at least several more days. "This will amplify the buildup of CO2 in the atmosphere driven by fossil fuel burning," said Richard Betts, the head of climate impacts research at the Met Office Hadley Centre. "The CO2 increase from this year to next will be about 3.5 parts per million, a third faster than in recent years and nearly twice as fast as what it should have been limited to if we'd been on track to limit global warming to 1.5C."
 
Zeke Hausfather, a climate researcher at Berkeley Earth, said: "Another day, another global temperature record," adding that the previous record of 2.05C over the 1850-1900 baseline, set in 2023, has been "smashed."

items.title: Suspected Chinese Agents Are Trying to Dupe Americans with Fake Listings on Job Platforms
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
"LinkedIn is probably the greatest intelligence tool that's ever been created," CNN heard from Holden Triplett, director of counterintelligence at the National Security Council in the first Trump administration. 

A LinkedIn spokesperson responded that "Creating a fake account or misrepresenting your identity is a clear violation of our terms of service." (And they also told CNN that LinkedIn remains "focused on detecting state-sponsored abuse and will continue to enforce our policies against fake accounts.") But it's not just happening on LinkedIn...



Suspected Chinese spies have created an elaborate web of fake firms with job opportunities aimed at tricking current and former US officials into divulging government secrets as part of a scheme that is more pervasive than previously reported, CNN has found. Interviews with a dozen people caught up in the operation — as well as CNN analysis of suspected bogus websites — reveal how there is a much broader target pool for obtaining sensitive US information after the Trump administration laid off thousands of federal employees. [CNN reported in 2025 that "foreign powers such as China and Russia" had directed their intelligence services "to ramp up recruiting of Americans working in national security by targeting those who had been fired or felt they were at risk of losing their jobs".] These workers left their posts with inadequate guidance and protection from spying plots, ex-officials said, creating a potentially valuable resource for Beijing and weak spot for Washington... In addition to government workers, the plot has targeted journalists, trade consultants and others, who might have knowledge deemed valuable to US adversaries. 

The FBI offered a glimpse into the malicious recruiting scam when it seized 13 websites officials say were tied to fake consulting firms in June. China denied the FBI allegations. CNN analyzed the sites' software code, looked at other suspicious job listings, and interviewed people approached by similar companies. CNN identified several more websites that mimicked the style and substance of those disabled by the FBI. Two more sites that Max Lesser, a senior analyst at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies think tank, discovered and shared with CNN have some of the same web infrastructure or other connections to the seized websites. In total, Lesser has uncovered more than 100 other web domains, many of which share similar characteristics with the sites taken down by the FBI.... 

This sprawling network has the hallmarks of a Chinese intelligence operation, Lesser told CNN. 

After creating fake web sites, the operatives "plant vague, well-paying job ads for consulting positions focused on China-related issues" on jobs sites like LinkedIn, CNN reports, asking applicants to produce "research reports". ("[D]ozens or hundreds of such reports, across various topics of interest to Beijing, can start to form a much clearer picture of US national security policy and its vulnerabilities, according to current and former FBI officials.") 

CNN sent a detailed request for a comment to a spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in Washington, DC. "I am not familiar with what you mentioned," they responded, adding that China "opposes vilifying China by peddling the so-called 'Chinese spy' narrative."

items.title: DOJ Again Admits To Lying As Yet Another Trump Revenge Prosecution Starts To Fall Apart
items.author: Tim Cushing
items.content:
The DOJ is nothing more than Trump’s revenge squad. Everyone Trump thinks has wronged him — whether it’s people who just weren’t loyal enough or people that engaged in investigations of his actions — is a target. That’s why Trump has pulled VP J.D. Vance from his peacekeeping mission in Iran to focus on “Democrat fraud.” That’s why the DOJ has been shedding talent since year one of Trump’s second term. And that’s why Trump has decided now is the time to see if he can’t turn Rep. Ilhan Omar into another one of his mass deportation victims.

United States President Donald Trump has called for Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar to resign from the US Congress, reviving allegations of identity fraud after a court filing identified the Minnesota politician by an additional name.

The DOJ filing, submitted on Wednesday, refers to Omar as “Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar” – “a/k/a” is an abbreviation for “also known as”.

The document filed by the administration does not establish that Omar committed fraud.

Oh, well. It didn’t stop a magistrate judge from approving a search warrant for Omar’s residence. And nothing seen so far indicates the federal court handling the (retaliatory) criminal case is ready to pull the plug on this bullshit.

But if there’s anything that’s going to kill Trump’s case dead, it will be whatever remains of his DOJ legal representation which has routinely misled courts and, in other cases, baldly admitted it no longer has the personnel to capably handle everything Trump wants it do. A DOJ stretched to the breaking point by mass deportation activities simply doesn’t have the spare cycles to slip retaliatory prosecutions of Trump’s enemies past the courts.

Once again, a federal court has caught the DOJ “misrepresenting” things in court, this time in relation to the ongoing investigation of Rep. Omar. “Caught” might be a bit too charitable to the court, since it was the admitting to malfeasance (but only after the court demanded more info from a DOJ that no longer has a healthy relationship with this part of the system of checks and balances).

The Justice Department admitted Tuesday that it misrepresented the position of the House’s top lawyer in multiple filings seeking to justify its handling of the Oct. 12 raid of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington residence.

Prosecutors told a magistrate judge that House General Counsel Matthew Berry “refused” to intervene in the search and instead endorsed the Trump administration’s view that searches of lawmakers’ private homes are not protected by the Constitution’s “speech or debate” clause, which shields lawmakers from prosecutorial scrutiny for their official conduct.

The DOJ might have gotten away with this lie if it weren’t for those meddling kids. Well… one meddling kid, specifically: House General Counsel Matthew Berry.

What the DOJ generously refers to as a “misrepresentation” is what everyone else would call a “lie.” Certainly the DOJ would call a misrepresentation a lie, especially if the misrepresentation occurred during a conversation with a federal officer.

But it gave itself a pass in its filing, because of course it did. It called the seemingly deliberate misrepresentation of Berry’s legal advice an “inadvertent misunderstanding.” That might be believable if all that came from it was some minor procedural errors. But what’s being justified here under the “oh no our reading comprehension” is the search of a congressional rep’s residence for the sole purpose of trying to find literally anything at all that might justify an expulsion from Congress and/or the United States itself.

In those filings, DOJ claimed Berry “refused to be involved,” and instead agreed with prosecutors’ view that lawmakers’ constitutional protections “do not extend to a Member’s private residence.”

But the exchange between Berry and McCotter shows a much more limited response than prosecutors portrayed.

Rather than embrace any limits on the “speech or debate” clause or its extension to private homes, Berry said House lawyers were not empowered to advocate for lawmakers who are the subject of criminal probes because their interests may diverge from the House’s. Had prosecutors searched a congressional office, Berry told McCotter, it would be more appropriate for his office to play a role. McCotter responded that evening: “Understood — Thanks for your time and consideration.” Twelve hours later, Department of Homeland Security agents arrived at Omar’s residence to carry out the search.

The House counsel said it was only likely to be involved in very specific situations. Berry may have agreed the “speech and debate” clause that generally provides immunity to congressional reps for their statements would (obviously) not shield them from a search of their residence if some criminal act was suspected. But Berry definitely say he supported or approved of any raid of Ilhan Omar’s home.

But the DOJ chose to say he did, hoping that paraphrasing an email from Berry would slid this past the magistrate judge and — beyond that — the judge handling the ensuing prosecution. But it didn’t work. And the moment others entered the fray to fight for the right to make Trump angry without being immediately subjected to a criminal investigation, the DOJ was forced to admit the stuff it said wasn’t honestly representative of the stuff it chose to misquote. And this seems like it’s going to result in another threat of sanctioning by yet another court.

And that’s because the DOJ is so compromised it can’t stop doing exactly this sort of thing. If the DOJ actually cared about justice, it wouldn’t need to lie nearly as often as it does. But since it’s just a floppy Trump appendage, this is just going to keep happening until Trump finally leaves office.

items.title: Anthropic, OpenAI Employees Fear Models Are Too Unsafe to Ever Release
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Axios reports:


Anthropic and OpenAI are facing an increasingly urgent problem: Internal, unreleased models are becoming so powerful that many employees no longer believe they can be safely released, according to more than two dozen sources familiar with the internal debates... 

The challenge could significantly slow the AI boom, as the gap between what the best AI systems can do and humans' ability to control them continues to widen, sources told Axios. 

Researchers haven't found technical solutions for controlling the most advanced models. Some insiders believe it's fixable. Others aren't convinced and say companies should stop training new models entirely... Anthropic and OpenAI have unreleased models that are far more powerful than what they've already released publicly, but the AI companies have struggled to ensure that they are safe enough for public release, sources said. This has led to debate within Anthropic, OpenAI and the AI research community about whether to stop releasing future frontier models publicly, instead reserving them for internal deployment only. 

There has also been debate around whether to train new models at all, sources inside and outside those companies told Axios.

items.title: Tuesday Jensen Huang Said Nvidia Doesn't Need a Succession Plan, and that He's in Therapy
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
CNBC reports:
[Jensen Huang] told staff that Nvidia has built a team that doesn't require succession planning the way a normal organization does, because the company operates a unique business model where there are multiple capable leaders at Nvidia that are leading different parts of the organization. A succession plan would create unnecessary hierarchy, Huang said, according to one of the people present... 

Huang told staff that Tuesday's company meeting was the second hardest meeting of his life, the first one being with his wife. He said he is in therapy, according to one of the people present.

items.title: Ohio’s Anti-SLAPP Law Works: Rep. Max Miller Loses Re-Election, Then His SLAPP Suit
items.author: Mike Masnick
items.content:
Ohio Rep. Max Miller seems like a pretty bad person. Despite years of reporting about his history as being abusive to women, the story seemed to finally break through earlier this year when Mother Jones did an incredible deep dive into the evidence on Miller’s abusive behavior towards his ex-wife, Emily Moreno (the daughter of Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno) and their 2-year-old child. Some of the reporting was absolutely stunning:

Records of the investigation into potential child abuse show that Moreno told detectives that Miller had previously thrown hot water at her, shoved her, and held a gun to her head; therefore, she couldn’t rule out that Miller caused their daughter’s fracture. Moreover, a child protection specialist reviewing the incident had characterized the bruising near the fracture as resembling a “handprint.”

“Daddy’s house is scary,” Moreno recounted her daughter saying, according to a Bay Village, Ohio,relating to the February 2026 injury.

The summary of the Zoom meeting andare among more than 2,000 pages of court filings and police reports pertaining to Miller that Mother Jones obtained through public records requests. The trove of documents contains allegations ofby Miller, misogyny and verbal abuse, and violent behavior against multiple women. The filings also includethat Miller implicitly threatened his ex-father-in-law, Sen. Bernie Moreno.

Some details had already come out a few months earlier, when the UK’s Daily Mail reported that Miller had been accused of “hurling a pot of boiling water” at Moreno, which already seemed pretty problematic. The further reporting from Mother Jones just served to further back up some of that original reporting.

Soon after that Daily Mail article came out in May, Miller filed an extremely ill-conceived SLAPP suit against his ex-wife and her lawyers. He argued that the story was part of the custody battle over the ex-couple’s child. Then, in August, Miller did a livestream on X denying the allegations and pointed viewers to a Dropbox folder that he said would exonerate him, stuffed with sensitive information about his family and the divorce and custody fight. But it also, somewhat horrifically, included an unredacted nude photo of their two-year-old child. Miller’s lawyer, Aaron Minc, admitted that he fucked up in including a photo of the naked child in the documents. Apology or not, Moreno sued Miller and Minc on their daughter’s behalf over the horrifying incompetence of releasing such a sensitive photo to the world.

Miller, who was up for re-election, kept insisting that this was all an attempt to harm his electability, and whether or not that was the case, he lost his re-election bid, fairly conclusively, getting 45.1% of the vote, compared to the winner, Brian Poindexter, who got 54.9%. That was a pretty big shift from two years earlier, when Miller defeated his then opponent by 15 points.

Then, less than two weeks later, the judge in the SLAPP suit he filed against his ex-wife threw out the case, and is making Miller pay up for her legal fees (he’d already dropped her lawyers from the case), thanks to Ohio’s recently passed anti-SLAPP statute. The judge pointed out that Miller failed to establish a prima facie case for defamation (as required under the anti-SLAPP law’s burden shifting), in part because there’s a recording of him admitting that he had, in fact, poured hot water on her:

An audio recording of the parties discussing the incident supports Defendant Moreno’s contention of truth. Defendant Moreno confronted Plaintiff about pouring “bowling [sic] hot water on me.” Although Plaintiff denies pouring hot water on her neck, he further admits the incident occurred. Plaintiff specifically stated “it was never done to hurt you with intent.” Plaintiff’s intent is irrelevant to the basic fact of whether the incident occurred, which addresses the element of falsity.

Plaintiff maintains that the gist or sting of hurling a pot of boiling water is “categorically different” than the actions Plaintiff states actually occurred. It is Plaintiff’s burden to support his claims with credible, admissible evidence. Plaintiff has not shown that the statement about dousing Defendant Moreno with boiling hot water are false. The imputation that Plaintiff poured or doused Defendant Moreno with hot water is substantially true.

Generally speaking, if there’s a recording of you admitting you did the thing you later sue someone for defamation over, it’s not going to go well for you.

And, thanks to the new anti-SLAPP law (which is based on the increasingly common UPEPA anti-SLAPP statute from the Uniform Law Commission), the judge orders Miller to pay $76,762.38 in his ex-wife’s legal fees.

So, in the course of less than two weeks, Miller lost his job and lost the bullshit vexatious lawsuit he filed against his ex-wife, for which he now needs to pay nearly $77k in her legal fees. Plus, the court found that the claim at the heart of his lawsuit, that he doused his ex-wife with hot water, is “substantially true.”

And, of course, he’s still facing that lawsuit over revealing a nude photo of his toddler, though the same week he lost his re-election bid, he filed his own motion to dismiss, including an anti-SLAPP motion against the state-law claims. In it, he argues that the federal claim fails because publishing the naked photo of his child related to “a matter of public concern” which strikes me as somewhat outlandish. His reasoning is that the image documents the injury at the heart of the abuse allegations, meaning that releasing it falls under the statute’s exception for “matters of public concern.”

Plaintiff now alleges that, even if the image was of public concern, the depicted anatomy was not, and that Defendants “could have redacted” it. But the exclusion turns on whether the action relates to a matter of public concern, not on whether each portion of an image was necessary to the speaker’s point. Plaintiff does not, and could not, allege that the disclosure of a document concerning the child’s injury, offered in response to public accusations about that injury, was unrelated to a matter of public concern.

When you find yourself arguing whether the naked image of your injured child that you released to the internet is or is not a matter of public concern, I’d say you’ve already lost.

items.title: FAA Identifies Patches for Last Week's Flight-Grounding Router Issue. But Was Staffing an Issue?
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
CNN published an exclusive report Tuesdayon what caused last week's nationwide ground stop for flights in the U.S.. A source familiar with the Federal Aviation Administration's investigation says they've recreated the issue in a lab "and believe they found the culprit."

Investigators have focused on determining why a new router at a remote Arkansas radio site overwhelmed the nation's air traffic control system with a massive amount of data, triggering gaps in radar and radio communications. They found an overlooked router setting affected how it interfaced with other decades-old routers that the FAA is decommissioning, the source said. Investigators believe software updates are needed and that those patches will prevent a repeat of the system failure... 

This month's ground stop not only focused attention on upgrades being made to the aging system, which have been paused as the agency investigated the incident, but also raised questions about FAA oversight of private companies charged with maintaining the network... On the day of the network meltdown, L3Harris was undertaking a maintenance job that involved switching the system from a decades-old router to a new one. In the past, this kind of work typically involved at least six FAA employees. Under the Trump administration, it's now often coordinated by one employee: an FAA liaison. And there are only four people in the country with that title, according to sources familiar with the process. 

The liaison's job involves coordinating and scheduling these upgrades — not approving them, sources said... The Trump administration's effort to move maintenance work along faster also eliminated a layer of FAA review that was critical to assessing risk [according to a source familiar with the process]. Previously, local technical operations managers, site technicians and others would determine when the work could be done with the least impact on air traffic and to game out worst-case scenarios. The union contends that process did not happen before L3Harris arrived at the El Dorado, Arkansas, site on November 13... [David Spero, president of the union], contends the FAA has given private companies "too much authority and generally unfettered access." 

CNN also points out a 2009 incident where 129 of America's air traffic facilities experienced an outage of FAA telecommunications "that delayed thousands of travelers and grounded hundreds of flights nationwide. 

"The cause: A technician with Harris Corp., which later merged with L3 Technologies to form L3Harris, incorrectly configured an FAA telecommunications router at the Los Angeles Center..."

items.title: The Birds Are Listening: Scientists Used Seabirds to Track Hidden Ships
items.author: Becky Ferreira
items.content:
, our newsletter about the most exciting and mind-boggling science news and studies of the week.

In what sounds like an avian riff on , scientists equipped seabirds with audio recorders in order to listen in on their interactions with fishing vessels across the world’s oceans, according to a study published on Wednesday in .

The approach exposed a large number of so-called “unseen” vessels that did not have their location trackers switched on. Many vessels are required to continuously signal their location using the Automatic Identification System (AIS), which openly broadcasts a ship’s location, similar to flight tracking. But AIS can be disabled for legitimate reasons—such as evading pirates—or with more nefarious motivations, such as concealment of illegal fishing activities. 

The new study was not designed to interrogate why any particular vessel switched off its AIS tracker. However, the discovery that seabirds are regularly interacting with unseen ships can shed light on broader efforts to monitor commercial fisheries, while also revealing new insights about seabird behavior, especially their risk of becoming “bycatch” when they are fatally trapped in fishing gear.

Unseen vessel activity “is concerning, or at least important, regardless of whether it's legal or illegal,” said Jonathan Rutter, a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of Oxford who led the study, in a call with 404 Media. He added that the recordings were not intended to be used for law-enforcement or surveillance, but that this line of research could become a “powerful tool for improving risk assessment” by recording seabird-vessel interactions that would otherwise be off the map. 

Rutter and his colleagues were inspired to combine these approaches by attaching audio recorders to three seabird species—the northern gannet, Balearic shearwater, and Westland petrel—which all frequently interact with fishing vessels. The team tracked the movements of the birds with GPS, and then analyzed whether the audio overlapped with AIS data at the same time and location during recorded interactions.

The recordings showed that about 32 percent of the audio captured by seven gannets in the North Atlantic were from ships with their trackers off, while 12 percent of the audio captured by four shearwaters in the Mediterranean Sea were from unseen vessels. The one petrel in the study interacted with vessels in the South Pacific, but its geolocation device was damaged, so it was not possible to calculate how many ships it encountered had their trackers off.

Rutter noted that the shearwaters were likely often interacting with smaller Mediterranean fishing boats that are not legally required to keep trackers on. However, the gannets encountered larger commercial vessels that are obligated to keep trackers active. While the researchers made a very conservative estimate that these birds visited unseen vessels for about one-third of the total duration of their daily encounters (or, about 22 minutes out of 68 minutes), it may well exceed half of that time.

“The fact that we found at least one third, and probably more than one half, of the audio detections being unseen was pretty surprising,” Rutter said. “This is not the same thing as saying that half of vessels are unseen; it's half of the time that gannets go to vessels, those vessels are unseen.”

“There are multiple reasons this could be,” he continued. “It could be illegal disabling, but at the same time, it could be poor satellite reception. There are lots of reasons that AIS can be off, and we want to emphasize that illegal fishing is a possibility, but that is not actually what we're showing. It's showing that there's a lot we're not seeing.”

Seabirds are attracted to fishing vessels to feed on discarded catch, but many perish during these encounters after becoming tangled in lines or caught on baited hooks. Rutter and his colleagues hope that their study could help to prevent these deadly incidents, while also providing a new tool for monitoring unseen vessel activity. 

While this approach could enable real-time vessel detection, the team urged “caution in the use of animals as a fisheries surveillance tool, lest fishers come to mistrust scientists and/or marine animals themselves,” according to the study.

Though environmental and commercial interests are often at odds, there is plenty of collaboration between fisheries and conservation scientists with the goal of sustainable and healthy long-term fish stock. Fisheries that adhere to regulations also have an interest in working with researchers to combat illegal activity by competitors.

In addition, these audio recordings offer a new way to eavesdrop on wild seabird behavior. For example, the petrel’s recordings captured distinct landing and takeoff sequences previously observed in albatrosses, opening a new avenue of research into the flight patterns of this species. The recordings also highlight how human activity has upended food webs, as seabirds have become dependent on fishing vessel waste as a major source of food. 

“One of the advantages of this is that we can understand in a more unbiased way how much [seabirds] actually interact with vessels—every day, multiple times a day for all the species we looked at actually, which is crazy if you think about it,” Rutter said. 

“They're going out every day and just visiting boats all the time, and that shows the impact that we have on them as humans is really changing their feeding ecology,” he concluded.

items.title: The New Robber Barons Aren’t Ready For The Fight
items.author: Anil Dash
items.content:
Ten years ago, I began writing a series about how we could move toward humane tech. Over the next year, I tried to get the people who build technology to look honestly at what the industry was becoming, while there was still time to change it. As you may be aware, that didn’t quite succeed.

Every once in a while, I’ll see people passing around links to some of those pieces, specifically to call out a couple of predictions that I made with the genuine hope that I would turn out to be wrong.

In a time of rising inequality, those who profit greatly while massively disrupting the stability of ordinary people tend to not be seen very kindly. The oil and steel barons of the past were seen as high tech innovators and valuable job creators for a while, until their excesses and abuses earned them a serious backlash.

That post was framed around a simple warning: unless people in tech became more self-critical, the industry’s leaders would come to be seen as the new robber barons. And then about six months later, in “How do we reform tech?”, I tried to say what was at stake if we didn’t:

The single biggest threat to the long-term health and growth of the tech sector is the backlash that could be caused by tech’s worst abuses and excesses.

At the time, plenty of people in the industry read those as the worries of a pessimist. That was also the era when tech’s most powerful voices (the investors who would have you believe that writing checks matters more than writing code) began a systematic campaign to undermine all criticism. They began to position journalists as their enemies, and said that anyone who was critical of tech leaders having absolute, unaccountable power over the economy and society was an enemy of progress, someone who hated innovation. It did not matter if, as was often the case, those of us who were being critical were actually creating innovations than the financiers who were pushing this big lie about tech criticism.

It may be hard to remember now, but a decade ago, tech was still treated as the unalloyed good guys. Founders and CEOs were the job creators and the inventors of the future, and politicians of every stripe were happy to be photographed next to tech’s biggest names. Media stories were framed around how parents would want their kids to be “the next Zuckerberg”.

As you may be aware, that is not the world we live in now.

We’ve arrived at the reckoning I was describing, and it’s worse than we’d have imagined. Tech’s most powerful voices have embraced authoritarianism wholesale, enthusiastically adopted an openly corrupt form of cronyism as central to their business models, and aggressively gone to war against their own workers (and labor in general) as part of a campaign to ensure that they’re never held accountable for any of the harms or wrongs that they cause. The result? A political environment where the largest tech companies and their founders are seen, accurately, as completely unregulated and unaccountable powers that inflict their will upon people across the world without consent or consideration.

The part I most wish I had gotten wrong is the last bit of the first quote. I said the robber barons of the past got their backlash “until their excesses and abuses earned them” one. I was hoping that the industry would choose to reform itself it got to that point. That was the entire point of all the writing and public speaking I did in that era.

But unfortunately, I failed. We weren’t able to stop the abuses. And now, the tech tycoons who’ve led us here are about to find out just how angry the world is at their abuses, their excesses, and their obvious attempts to show the rest of society that they are above the law and any moral or ethical rules.

Things are not going to go the way that they think.

Just how bad it gets is going to depend on how quickly they understand just how poorly they’ve read the room. As I keep pointing out, hundreds of thousands of tech workers have lost their jobs; when I wrote about it at the beginning of the year, it was half a million — now it’s closer to a million.

None of those ordinary tech workers lost their jobs because they were having inappropriate relationships with a subordinate, or because they had bribed the President of the United States with tens of millions of dollars, or because they had a sexual relationship with a foreign asset that compromised national security. But they can see that someone can get away with of those harms, and still have a job paying unimaginable riches, even while decent people are struggling to get by. They will not miss the lesson that’s being taught.

I don’t take any pleasure in having called this one. If anything, it makes the case for the rest of what I wrote back then stronger, not weaker. The reforms I was asking for in 2016 are no more radical now, and they are far more urgent. And the people inside the industry who still care about doing right by the world have a much stronger argument to push for change than they did a decade ago, because the alternative is being lumped in with the tycoons who are feverishly working to become the most hated people in the world.

If you’ve been waiting for a sign that it’s time to speak up, you’re out of excuses. The backlash that’s coming is going to be extreme. And I know that because all we have to do is look at the time there was a class of robber barons who abused their power to this degree. Those tycoons probably controlled of the economy, and had less of an obvious impact on people’s day-to-day lives, and yet the reason they ended up funding all those libraries and museums we see today is because they spent enough years dodging bombing attacks and assassination attempts that they finally realized something had to change. I would love to see today’s tycoons invest in the public sphere in order to rehabilitate their image, but they’ve already shown that their preference is to double down on shamelessly acting like they’re untouchable.

Perhaps they really are above any accountability. We will certainly find out.

Everyone is going to have to pick a side on today’s robber barons. I think they’re in such an isolated and extreme cultural and media bubble that they genuinely don’t understand how wildly unpopular they are. But for ordinary tech workers, and the people affected by the decisions that these tycoons make, now is the time to make clear which side you’re on. The lessons of the past are clear: you will not want to side with the people who are willing to shamelessly abuse others and assume that the chickens will never come home to roost.

items.title: Those Five Tons of Bomb-Making Chemicals in Iowa Will Be Detonated Wednesday Morning
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
The detonation is back on. Nearly five tons of unstable lead azide explosives will be detonated Wednesday morning at a U.S. Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, reports the Iowa Capital Dispatch (part of the nonprofit States Newsroom network 

"The scheduled time follows numerous delays over the past week from the Army, a lawsuit, intervention from the president, and widespread public concern of the health and environmental effects associated with detonating a lead-based explosive."

Lead deposition maps released by the Army Tuesday morning show lead released by the detonation could be dispersed in the air as far as 100 miles southwest of Middletown and cross into Missouri. An additional map shows there is a potential for lead surface dust to settle as far as 50 miles southwest of the detonation site. The Army has recommended, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency is supporting, the evacuation of Iowans in Middletown and the immediate area — a 5-mile cone to the southwest of the detonation site — during the detonation period. Soldiers, environmental teams and other federal officials are in the area helping to sample soils and alert residents of the detonation plans... 

A slew of federal officials from the Army, the EPA, Department of Health and Human Services, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms, Department of Agriculture and more gathered at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant Tuesday for a press conference and shared new information with the public about the response... Speaking at the press conference Tuesday, Sean Kaufman with HHS said the highest risk is for pregnant individuals, children, or people with chronic illnesses who live or plan to be in the areas the Army forecasts will be impacted. "You definitely want to be out of that area," Kaufman said of the at-risk groups. "I would evacuate that area that's signaled in the model... " As many as 100 Iowa National Guard soldiers will be available to aid local, state and federal agencies in their public safety plans [according to a news release from the governor]. They will also help provide guidance and assistance to around 150 households with a temporary evacuation... 

At the news conference, acting Secretary of the Army Hon. Adam Telle emphasized that the government's priority was the "health and safety of the citizens of this region." Telle said those involved have sought advice from "every expert" in and outside of the federal government and have considered all viable options and data before reaching the conclusion to proceed with detonation.
"There is consensus across the experts across the country that a controlled, mitigated detonation of the lead azide here at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, is far preferable to an uncontrolled spontaneous detonation of that substance," Telle said. Some of those mitigations include: sand around the structure holding the barrels; two walls of four, 16,000-gallon water tanks; a plan to "flood" the exterior of the storage area with aqueous foam to help absorb particulate matter from the blast; and modeling to forecast impacted areas based on weather conditions.

items.title: I Listened to ‘Sandstorm’ Through a Sex Toy
items.author: Samantha Cole
items.content:
You don’t really realize how much downtime there is in the song “Sandstorm” by Darude until you’re waiting for the bass to drop while it’s playing inside your vagina. 

In August 2025, I got an email with the subject line “‘Airpods for your @ss’ raises nearly half a million in Kickstarter campaign.” I get a lot of zany pitches for products that don’t exist yet, and a lot of pitches for products that do exist but perhaps should not. This one was for a device called the , a sex toy that turns music into vibration patterns. But the pitch didn’t include the phrase “sex toy” at all. Instead, it’s called an “internal music player.” 

I asked for a unit to review, expecting this to be purely conceptual. But they had one, and offered to send it. “The prototype functions very similarly to the final product but we do want to stress it’s a garage built prototype,” the rep for Groove Thing told me. I thought for a moment about putting something “garage built” and connected to a wall outlet into an orifice and passed. While , I decided to wait until the version they planned to send to customers in the fall was ready. 

The production-ready Groove Thing arrived at my doorstep last month in an intimidatingly large box. The configuration consists of a fairly hefty speaker that’s meant to sit on your nightstand, an AC power cable, and a “resonator base,” which connects to the speaker with a pinned cord. It also came with three attachment shapes: vaginal, anal, and external (a vac-u-lock adapter is available separately for attaching your own dildos to the base). The attachment shapes are made of hard plastic, not the soft, flexible silicone I’m used to in a sex toy. They lock onto the resonator with a twist. 

Opening the box and feeling the hard, inflexible plastic raised my skepticism that this thing would be comfortable. Most sex toys are covered in silky silicone that offers a little flexibility and give. But as I’m told over and over by the pamphlets that come in the box, Groove Thing “isn’t a vibrator.” Groove Thing inventor Michael Weiss-Malik, who co-founded it with Elizabeth Dell, told me it’s hard plastic for a reason, and is the result of testing feedback from the around 180 people they handed a prototype before putting it on the market.

“We started with off-the-shelf silicone dongs, and they were already producing an interesting experience for people,” Weiss-Malik told me on a call. “But we experimented with different types of materials, and what we found was that the silicone transmitted way fewer ranges of frequencies than hard plastic, and the hard plastic produces much higher fidelity.” 

The mechanism that vibrates the base to the beat of the music is also different from most other sex toys on the market today, Weiss-Malik said. But he declined to share what actually runs the toy, beyond mysteriously stating it’s not “a motor.” Weiss-Malik is a former NASA engineer, where he worked on the software that helped map Mars. He’s also worked at Google, where he worked on Earth mapping software, and previously worked leadership roles at Uber and Cruise, the self-driving car company General Motors later acquired and ultimately shut down after a serious accident. But he’s been involved in the sex positive community in the San Francisco bay area “for going on 20 years,” he told me, and is the type of guy to pop into a sex shop anytime he passes one when traveling. All of this taken together makes a lot of sense to me, given that he’s the kind of guy to spend a summer between jobs tinkering in his garage, designing a device that could put music up your ass. 

“Groove Thing doesn't use a motor. We don't say what is in there, but it's not a motor,” he said. “It uses a different set of physics that's more similar to audio equipment, and as a result, it can actually reproduce a full sound form, not just an on-off. You know, a sound-responsive vibrator is mostly just an on-off switch that's connecting to the beat.” Other vibrating sex toys work in that way: An eccentric rotating mass motor spins, turning pre-programmed patterns into vibration. Handheld sex toy makers have to work around several factors, including the limits of these motors, the tendency of soft silicone to dampen vibration, and the shapes they need to compact them into to fit in a device that doesn’t wear out customers’ wrists. Groove Thing seems to get around some of these problems by skipping the typical rotating motor, shaping the attachments in such a way that you can insert them and then go mostly hands-free when lying down, and choosing a plastic that feels kind of awkward at first.

The combination means different instruments and ranges come through as different levels of vibration. “A piano or bass guitar feels different than a drum kit. It almost feels like having a third ear,” Weiss-Malik said. “There's a level of fidelity there, where you have a whole new dimension to the sound that you're hearing. It works particularly well in bass, but it works all the way up to the mid frequencies.” Groove Thing replicates frequencies you can’t hear with your ears, he said — kind of like being at a concert and standing close enough to the stack that you feel it in your chest. As someone who recently almost lost their eyebrows and gained tinnitus at a Mogwai show, I get it, and I think for most people this comparison is what will make the Groove Thing click for them.  

”Some of what you're feeling is subsonic; it's down below 20 hertz, and we actually reproduce that as well,” Weiss-Malik said. “So you actually experience parts of your music that you never even noticed were there before, or that your ears can't hear, and that at the very least, home stereo equipment has a very hard time reproducing. So you're getting an experience that hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of speakers are normally required for you to get that out of the recording.” This was my experience with “Sandstorm.” You wouldn’t believe how much not-music is going on in that song, but also, how the moments that seem like they should be intense rumbly bass-drops are actually at a higher register. 

The creators of Groove Thing want you to be able to play whatever you want, which you can from your phone via Bluetooth or the optional aux jack, but they also really, really want you to try their intro playlist, I assume to prevent people like myself from putting “Crab Rave” on the stereo and then writing it off as a bust. is eclectic, beginning with “Beads on the Wind: The Human Experience Remix” and “Aya,” which I would place in a repeat-Burning-Man-attendee genre (no judgement here), but continues into “Blinding Lights” by The Weeknd and, to my pleasant surprise, an underrated track from Taylor Swift’s album, “I Think He Knows.” An with more songs features mostly EDM but also throws “Piece of Me” by Britney Spears in there. 

This entire test run of this not-vibrator made me, an admittedly tone deaf and musically unsophisticated person (see the previous lines), realize how much is happening in music that I’m never picking up with my own two ears. The “third ear” analogy is pretty spot-on: To enjoy the Groove Thing with an open mind, you have to let go of the typical expectations of other sex tech. Climax isn’t the point. The point is to use your junk to go on a musical journey, which is something that will resonate strongly for some, and miss others. 

“You know, people don’t go to a concert just to hear the finale and go home. Groove Thing isn’t a tool like most vibrators are,” Weiss-Malik told me. “It's more like a concert experience. You get to bask in pleasure for a period of time. In our early beta tester groups, most people who had unlimited usage of it used it for over an hour in their first session. Most of the second time users in that beta group also used it for over an hour in their second session.” 

The entire sex tech market has been trending away from the literal, anatomical, and climax-centered for years, with more toys coming in abstracted colors, shapes, and features that focus on pleasure and experience over getting your own personal money shot. I see Groove Thing as a logical step in that evolution.

Groove Thing is shipping out orders as of this month, and retails at $369 for the single unit and more for add-ons and additional units for partnered play.

items.title: Trump FCC (AT&T) Says California Can’t Enforce Its Broadband Protection And 911 Reliability Laws
items.author: Karl Bode
items.content:
As the federal U.S. government has given up on consumer protection and corporate oversight, states have filled the void with various degrees of success. That’s been particularly apparent in areas like telecom, where the corruption-fueled death of federal privacy and net neutrality protections have been replicated in a handful of states like California, which passed their own state-level laws.

This year, the Trump administration told California that it can’t enforce any of its own consumer protection laws if it wants to receive $1.4 billion Congress already earmarked for broadband expansion under the 2021 infrastructure bill. It’s extortion on behalf of regional telecom giants eager to see less and less oversight of their predatory business practices in uncompetitive markets.

Now the Trump FCC is again directly backing AT&T, and demanding that California can’t enforce its own Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules. These COLR rules mandate that state residents have reliable access to voice calls, 911, deaf and disabled assistance services, customer service support, protection from unwanted charges, and flexible billing options.

A new order by Brendan Carr’s FCC grants AT&T’s request to pre-empt all state consumer protection rules. It’s a giant hand out to unpopular telecom monopolies, misleadingly framed by Carr as a “modernization” of “outdated regulation” (that just so happens to ensure people don’t die as a result of not being able to reach 911):

“California’s Carrier of Last Resort framework may have made sense when it was established 30 years ago. But those rules were designed for a bygone era and no longer make sense in today’s competitive, advanced marketplace.”

That all rules and regulations shitty telecom monopolies say are “outdated” and must be “modernized to protect innovation” is an industry lie that captured regulators have been parroting for most of my adult life. As is any claim that U.S. telecom is remotely “competitive.”

AT&T lobbyists have worked tirelessly to eliminate such requirements in 20 of its 21 state service territories, falsely claiming the regulations stifled the company’s ability to install next-generation fiber. In reality, AT&T has long been criticized for cheaping out on fiber investments, and is primarily interested in eliminating already dwindling oversight on both the state and federal levels.

In countless communities where AT&T cheaped out on fiber investments and upgrades (despite spending untold billions on doomed media mergers), they’ll insist that 5G wireless is “good enough.” But 5G still doesn’t uniformly reach many parts of the state, and as AT&T has hung up on aging DSL lines, many communities are being left without access to essential online services, or life-saving 911 support.

While most states and the federal government have basically abandoned telecom and broadband consumer protection, California remains an outlier. The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) has been doing some amazing work on trying to ensure that broadband is both reliable and affordable, something lumbering monopolies simply refuse to accept.

While California’s efforts are mischaracterized as “extreme” by industry and our captured regulators, these kind of bare-minimum quality control standards are commonplace in most developed countries. Increasingly, the U.S. struggles to insist it’s a developed country, with corruption hollowing out already shaky regulatory autonomy and corporate oversight.

Telecom monopolies have had an intimate ally in the Trump administration, which has repeatedly declared that government effort to ensure your shitty local cable or phone company isn’t ripping you off is “woke.” With so much else going on, the efforts have been a broad success (for AT&T, Comcast, Charter, and Verizon), with little meaningful attention from a consolidated U.S. corporate press.

items.title: Is Nvidia's Legal Trouble Over - Or Just Beginning?
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
America's Justice Department "is still investigating Nvidia," reports the New York Post, adding that Monday President Trump posted on Truth Social that Nvidia should also "continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company's compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security." 

But President Trump also told The New York Post Monday in an exclusive interview "that he's willing to pardon Jensen Huang if necessary — but that he believes the reinstalled Nvidia CEO should be fine without one and should 'tell the truth' to Congress when he testifies next week...

Huang doesn't need to invoke his Fifth Amendment rights to avoid self-incrimination when he sits for an interview with the House Foreign Affairs Committee next Tuesday and appears before a hearing of the Senate Banking Committee next Thursday, Trump added... 

The president said that Nvidia's success was essential to the US retaining an edge in artificial intelligence — and that he's even open to the company giving the American government an equity stake, noting Intel handed over 10% of its value last year. "I thought about it. I said, 'You know, maybe I should do it,' but I didn't bring it up at this point. It's probably not too late," Trump said. 

Earlier a source familiar with Jensen Huang's comeback "told the New York Post that President Trump and Vice President Vance 'became convinced that Jensen was a singular figure protecting Open Source models and preventing the closed-source model companies from becoming too powerful.'" 

And CBS News reports that Nvidia's Jensen Huang "still has security clearance, sources say." (Although revoking Huang's clearance "was discussed..."

It is not uncommon for executives at tech companies that do classified federal work to have security clearances... [U.S. Attorney General Todd] Blanche said the government relies on a "collective consensus" among federal agencies to assess national security risks and determine whether somebody is able to access sensitive government information. 

An Nvidia spokesperson declined to comment on Huang's clearance. 
Asked whether the Justice Department investigated Jensen Huang before Mr. Trump assured Nvidia's board that he had not engaged in wrongdoing, Blanche said he would have informed the president if the department had evidence Huang had committed a crime. "To the extent that that Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes or something like this ... that's something that I would have certainly told the president had it been true," Blanche said. Pressed on how the department could rule out potential criminal liability while export-control investigations remained ongoing, Blanche said he could not predict whether future investigations might produce different findings. 
"I can't predict the future," Blanche said.
 

Jensen Huang is still testifying before the U.S. Congress next week, reports The Hill:


The Republican chairs of three different House committees stressed the need to address concerns regarding national security despite Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO.. "The NVIDIA board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast (R-Fla.), House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party Chair John Moolenaar (R-Mich.) and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) wrote in a joint statement obtained by NewsNation... 
"We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of NVIDIA products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary's AI capabilities," it continued.

 

U.S. Senators are also promising to grill Nvidia's Jensen Huang, reports Politico, and to pass new legislation regulating future chip exports:

"The controversy with Nvidia ... is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back," Senate Intelligence Chair Tom Cotton posted Monday. "Congress has much to investigate," he said, "and we will pass overwhelmingly bipartisan chip export-control bills, including my Chip Security Act, one way or the other." Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter is also expected to testify Dec. 2, and one House Democratic aide said lawmakers are already "considering" asking other Nvidia board members to provide information.... 

Sen. Kevin Cramer, a member of Senate Banking, predicted that between Democrats outraged by Trump's backing of Huang and GOP wariness toward China, an export control measure would pass by a margin large enough "to overcome a veto." Even if Huang ends up not participating in the hearings, or if Republicans back away under pressure from Trump, Democrats like incoming Banking Chair Elizabeth Warren could turbocharge their investigation plans using their new subpoena powers next year. "Chairman Elizabeth Warren and a number of Banking Committee Republicans ... are going to put the screws to these people like they've never had the screws put to them before," Cramer said in an interview. 
Jensen Huang's scandal revealed that American export-control policy "remains riddled with loopholes, hobbled by incapacity and infighting, and divorced from clear strategy," according to Foreign Affairs (the magazine published by the nonprofit Council on Foreign Relations think tank). 
While the magazine applauded a recent tightening of restrictions, it suggests more action from Congress since the current administration's "lax enforcement of past controls — and internal divisions over the new ones — raise serious questions about its willingness to follow through."
As a starting point, Congress should pass the Remote Access Security Act, which would give the administration clear legal authority for controlling remote access to data centers powered by U.S. compute. While implementation will require close congressional oversight, getting the right legal structure in place is an important first step. Next, it should work with industry and technical experts to fund and fast-track "on-chip" technologies — basically, features that can verify a chip's location and counter smuggling and diversion. Beyond sorting out the technical feasibilities, Congress will need to work with industry to understand the implications of on-chip security mechanisms for global competitiveness and the potential surveillance risks should China develop similar controls since it produces much of the world's legacy chips. Along with these technical fixes, Congress should seize on the Megaspeed scandal to strengthen oversight. The AI Overwatch Act, which may be included in the annual defense bill, would codify existing export controls on advanced chips into law, preventing the current or a future administration from reversing them. It would also empower Congress to review and block advanced chips sales to U.S. adversaries. 

Congress can go even further by establishing a new investigative committee or inspector general to strengthen oversight of sensitive chip export-control policies. [Another suggestion the article makes? "[C]ondition advanced chip sales on the buyer's ability to protect them from diversion and guard against misuse by malign actors looking to skirt safety and security rules."] Together, these actions would go a long way toward combating the circumvention that let firms such as Megaspeed thrive... Congress has a role in ensuring that the president faithfully executes the laws and is supported by the right resources, oversight, and strategic priorities. The United States' AI lead may hinge on whether it meets the moment.
