items.title: Amazon Drone Crashes On Garage After Delivering Shampoo, Draws FAA Probe
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has opened an investigation into an Amazon Prime Air delivery drone that struck a fiber-optic cable and crashed onto a residential garage in Michigan after delivering shampoo. The drone lost a propeller and became entangled in power lines, prompting Amazon and local utility workers to coordinate its removal. Amazon offered to help repair the damaged roof and gave the homeowner a $100 gift card. Ars Technica reports: Amazon Prime Air currently operates a fleet of battery-powered MK30 drones that can deliver packages weighing up to five pounds and have onboard sense-and-avoid technology to avoid obstacles. However, the drone clearly failed to avoid the thin fiber-optic cable in this case -- so hopefully the FAA investigation would take that into account along with Amazon delivery drone procedures.
 
The FAA preliminary accident and incident notification briefly describes the incident as "UAS struck a fiber cable, a residential garage, and became entangled in power lines during takeoff." That notice was posted on November 23. The National Transportation Safety Board is also gathering information about the incident but has not yet decided whether to open its own probe, according to CNBC. That US government agency holds primary responsibility for investigating aviation accidents and other transportation incidents. 
Amazon said the Michigan crash was the first involving its drone delivery operations near Detroit, but federal regulators are already investigating several incidents in Arizona and Texas involving collisions with a construction crane, an internet cable, and an apartment building.
 
An Amazon spokesperson said Prime Air drones make nearly 6,000 flights per day and have delivered "hundreds of thousands of packages this year."

items.title: Experts: It Will Take Years & A New President To Regain Our Measles Elimination Status
items.author: Timothy Geigner
items.content:
I’ve been writing about the ongoing measles outbreak in America since March of 2025, and first began predicting we would lose our measles elimination status in April of 2025. While America did recently lose that status, I’m no Nostradamus. I simply watched how the case counts continued to rise at increasing rates and then watched what the federal government did about it, which was mostly fuck-all. It didn’t require any clairvoyance to see where this was heading.

But now that we’ve lost our elimination status… how do we get it back? The answer is obvious: vaccinations. It was a massive vaccination campaign that gained us elimination status in 2,000, after all. But even if we all accept that as the right answer, what’s it going to take to get it done? According to at least one expert, the answer is several years and a new president.

The PBS post above goes into great detail about how the measles came back and the history of how we eliminated it previously. Then it talks about how to regain that status.

[Professor William] Moss said that, while it’s impossible to predict when or if the U.S. will regain the status, he would expect it to take around five years and a different presidential administration. He said the Trump administration’s undermining of vaccines counteracts the efforts needed to regain measles elimination status.

“I don’t see them completely turning around and giving the messaging and support that we would need to regain elimination status in the next two years,” he said. “It would take a new administration and a real focus on clear messaging about the value of vaccines and the measles vaccine in particular.”

Take a moment to realize how damning and pathetic that statement is. How do we re-eliminate a deadly disease for which we have the tools at hand? Well, obviously we need to wait until the idiot leader that’s in charge is gone, of course. A more clear demonstration for the need to get rid of RFK Jr. from HHS I couldn’t come up with oh my own.

But the reason a new administration is necessary to do the work on this is because the cure for our measles outbreaks is vaccination. Specifically childhood vaccination, which the current president and Kennedy won’t advocate for because your children should have the freedom to die with angry rashes on their skin.

Dr. Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO’s Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization, said the U.S. and other countries that lost their elimination status are expected to present corrective plans outlining the strategies they will take to regain that status.

To do that, the U.S. needs to increase its vaccine coverage, identify cases quickly, track people who have been in contact with infected patients and respond rapidly to outbreaks, Gordon said.

Roess said requiring vaccines for children entering schools is key to protecting communities from measles.

“The key is to make this required with very few exemptions,” she said.

I can’t see any of that being done under the Trump administration, even if he launched Kennedy, which I also don’t expect to happen. That means the next two years could get very dark from a measles and health perspective, which I expect might elongate the timeline further for getting our elimination status back.

This is all so needless, it’s infuriating.

items.title: US Spy Agencies Suffer Breach of Some Unclassified Information
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: The Central Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence recently discovered a cybersecurity breach that exposed some of their unclassified information, according to U.S. officials and other people familiar with the matter. The intrusions affected an open-source intelligence analysis system, a computer network that looks for intelligence insights in public, unclassified material, the people familiar with the issues said. It was not clear specifically what information was compromised, but classified material was not jeopardized, the people said. Information at other government agencies was also believed to have been exposed in the breach, according to two of the people.
 
Open-source intelligence can include vast troves of commercially available data sets, social media content, satellite imagery and other online material. Much of it is publicly available, but it can include information sold by data vendors that can be highly revealing, especially when combined with other tranches of data. Spy agencies can also use the data alongside other sources of intelligence to inform analytical judgments. It is not uncommon for federal agencies to suffer cybersecurity breaches, but several have recently detected intrusions into some of their systems, prompting heightened concern among current and former U.S. intelligence officials. When asked about the recent hack of the FBI crime database, Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, said breaches occurred frequently and that there was no cause for alarm. "Cyberprobing, cyberincidents, they have been part of the American economy, part of the American life for a long time."
 
"And what we're hearing about the F.B.I., and what I've talked to them about is, they have an incident. They're dealing with it in the ordinary course."

items.title: Spotted On The D.C. Metro: Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveals Plan For Smithsonian Overhaul
items.author: Andy Kroll
items.content:
Since the Trump administration erupted this summer with criticism of the Smithsonian National Museum of American History for promoting “radical activist ideology” and precipitated the departure of Smithsonian secretary Lonnie Bunch, the White House’s next step on this front of the culture wars has been unclear.

Now the plan may have been revealed — inadvertently — in a crowded car on Washington, D.C.’s Metro transit system.

In the last week of October, as political Washington was focused on the coming midterm elections, a commuter on the Orange Line from the Northern Virginia suburbs was startled to see displayed, on the laptop of a man seated adjacent in a gray tartan suit, a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan.” The commuter snapped a few phone photos over the man’s shoulder and dispatched them to ProPublica.

The 25-item list laid bare a comprehensive effort to completely transform the history museum, which employs several hundred people, is home to several million artifacts and draws close to 2 million visitors per year. If implemented in anything like the proposed form, it would represent an unprecedented assertion of White House control over the Smithsonian, which is structured to be independent.

Among the actions listed on the plan: firing the museum’s director, Anthea Hartig, and a dozen other top administrators and curators; announcing a new permanent exhibit called “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance” and an exhibit on “Great Families of American History”; and announcing a new “Colossus Statue” of George Washington for the museum’s entrance.

Other items on the list harkened back to a scathing 162-page critique of the museum released by the White House on July 4. That report was followed by back-to-back congressional hearings and a Trump executive order requiring signs to be erected outside the museum warning about the “ideological capture” on display there. While the pressure helped prompt Bunch’s departure as head of the Smithsonian, the warning signs have yet to go up, and it was unknown exactly what fixes the White House had in mind for the flaws that it so loudly decried.

Until now, perhaps. The plan displayed on the staffer’s laptop would issue new interpretative guidelines for exhibits, ending the museum’s reliance on a diversity style guide. It would review the Smithsonian’s strategy for traveling exhibitions, including halting one now underway, “The Bias Inside Us.” It would review the Smithsonian’s financial grants to “woke third parties” such as the American Alliance of Museums. And it would overhaul the museum’s online K-12 curriculum to “realign educational materials with patriotism, not ideology.” For instance, the website would drop the “Becoming US” module on immigration and launch a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage.”

The plan was apparently still a work in progress, given that the staffer had scribbled other proposals on a sheet of paper, also in plain view. They included “announce exciting cool exhibit on D-Day” and “no X rated exhibitions policy.” The latter item was a likely reference to something that drew a great deal of opprobrium in the July report and two congressional hearings that followed: a gay history exhibit that included a two-piece chrome and rubber crotch harness designed for sadomasochism.

At first, the identity of the staffer was undetermined, beyond a few clues including the fact that his initials were either B.S. or S.B., as displayed on his laptop. ProPublica reporters scoured White House staffing records to narrow down the list of candidates and took to the Orange Line to see if he would pop up again. Sure enough, there we saw the likeliest candidate, carrying the same style of brown leather satchel and same type of phone. He disembarked in Washington for the short walk to a White House employee checkpoint. It was Sam Bock, a 27-year-old associate policy adviser with the Domestic Policy Council, the White House office that produced the July report.

The White House did not respond to a query about the draft plan. Bock, who previously worked on the staff of Rep. Jim Jordan, the Ohio Republican elected last week as House Minority Leader, did not respond to messages. The Smithsonian, which bid farewell to Bunch at a board meeting last month, declined to comment.

The Smithsonian encompasses 20 museums beyond the American history one. It has a 17-member board that is led by the chief justice of the Supreme Court and comprises the U.S. vice president, three members of Congress from each party and nine private citizens nominated by other board members. But it relies on the federal government for the majority of its funding, receiving more than $1 billion per year, and its leadership is in a state of flux: Not only is it seeking to replace Bunch, but the board itself is riddled with vacancies as private citizen terms expire without replacements. Until President Donald Trump attempted to fire the director of the National Portrait Gallery last year, no president had tried to remove a Smithsonian executive. (The institution resisted, but the director, Kim Sajet, decided to leave anyway.)

As recounted by ProPublica in September, the American history museum has faced scrutiny over the years. Since its founding in 1964, it has struggled with the mission of telling the story of a vast and variegated nation; in 2001, an earlier round of criticisms prompted a blue-ribbon commission to produce a report urging the museum to offer a more unified approach to the national story, with fewer nods to political correctness. The Smithsonian underwent another identity crisis following the murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis in 2020, as Bunch and others led an institution-wide self-reckoning.

By the time of Trump’s return to office in 2025, there was no shortage of fodder for the new administration to seize on. The July report noted a recent exhibit on Ben Franklin that speculated about whether he had used enslaved members of his household as subjects of his experiments with electric shocks. And it chastised the museum for having trained staff using the “Museums as a Site for Social Action Toolkit,” a 200-plus-page tract on how to “truly transform the museum space,” which it says is linked “with white supremacy, hetero-patriarchy, abuse of labor, colonization, imperialist theft of art and artifacts, destruction or absencing of alternative ways of interpreting or representing art and artifacts, structural racism and other oppressions.”

The White House report emphasized that the museum should not whitewash blights on the nation’s history such as slavery and Jim Crow, but argued that it was failing to give visitors any sense of how it developed into the country that it is. “It should tell the whole story of a nation,” the report stated, “including the good and the bad, so Museum visitors can understand the development that led our nation to where it is today.”

The report was released with symbolic fanfare on the 250th anniversary of the nation’s founding. The administration’s announcement of its next move on this front may have less pop, given its soft rollout on the Orange Line.

items.title: Hackers Compromise Check Point Servers In 22 Organizations
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Hackers have compromised 24 Check Point Security management servers across 22 organizations in 17 countries in a suspected cyberespionage campaign, according to threat intelligence firm GreyNoise. BleepingComputer reports: The researchers track the activity as GT13 and confirmed it was ongoing between October 17 and November 2, when their visibility ended. However, given the threat actor's persistent access to Check Point devices, they believe the campaign remains active. GreyNoise says the 22 victim organizations are spread across 17 countries, and show no clear evidence of specific targeting. They include government entities, financial services providers, and companies in the energy, transportation, mining, and manufacturing sectors. The attacks were launched from 99 IP addresses that appear to come from compromised Check Point devices and ExpressVPN exit nodes.
 
A Rejetto HTTP File Server, compromised by exploiting CVE-2026-61500, was used as an operational relay for managing intrusions and collecting stolen data from the compromised environments. While GreyNoise could not determine when or how the Check Point servers were breached, it observed the exploitation of CVE-2026-16232 during the post-compromise stages. The vulnerability is an authentication bypass in Check Point SmartConsole that allows attackers to obtain an application login token and authenticate with administrator privileges. Check Point warned about the flaw in July, marking it as an actively exploited zero-day. The researchers also observed attempts to exploit CVE-2025-5777 (Citrix NetScaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti), CVE-2026-41089 (Windows NetLogon), CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), and CVE-2026-98432 (Linux IPv4 UAF).

items.title: The Global War On VPNs Draws Closer
items.author: Glyn Moody
items.content:
Back in March, Walled Culture noted that companies were increasing their attacks on VPNs, in part because of claims that the latter were being widely used for the circumvention of copyright law. Unfortunately, since then the trend discussed there has continued, with a notable uptick in recent months. For example, the LaLiga professional association football league in Spain, which has appeared a number of times on this blog, has called for major VPNs to be placed on the European Union’s “Counterfeit and Piracy Watch List”. TorrentFreak explains:

The 14-page submission targets a wide range of sites and services, including traditional piracy threats, but the VPN section is new. The league notes that it doesn’t take offense with the technology itself, but with how these providers are marketed by others through their affiliate programs.

That may be so, but putting VPN providers on “counterfeit and piracy watch lists” is a slippery slope. Once the precedent is established, it will be easy for others to claim that the marketing of a VPN provider is somehow promoting copyright infringement. And once VPNs are officially associated with breaking the law in this way, it will be natural to attack them more vigorously.

That is what is beginning to happen in the US, with a number of legislative proposals that would impact VPNs. For example, the absurdly named “Shielding Children’s Retinas from Egregious Exposure on the Net Act” or the “SCREEN Act”. The EFF explains that the main aim of the bill is to require online services to verify users’ ages before they can access any sexually explicit content. But VPNs are explicitly targeted:

The bill requires covered websites to verify users’ ages based on their IP addresses unless the service can determine that the user is outside the United States, and specifically requires age verification on traffic coming from known VPN addresses. In practice, this discourages the use of VPNs and proxy servers, which millions of people rely on for legitimate purposes such as protecting personal privacy, securing public Wi-Fi connections, safeguarding journalists and activists, and preventing data tracking.

Under the ACPA, any broadband provider, DNS resolver, or VPN with 100,000 or more monthly users or subscribers in the United States can be named in a blocking order. Smaller services are exempt, as well as root nameservers and top-level domain registries.

Interestingly, a “competing” site-blocking proposal is notable for not including VPNs in its scope:

The DEFEND IP Act explicitly excludes services that exclusively provide VPN connections or similar encrypted routing, as well as DNS services that only work through encrypted protocols, such as DoH.

That’s welcome, but it’s not yet clear which of those differing approaches, if any, will become law. Meanwhile, it is only too clear that VPNs are already under attack. This has prompted some pushback from the Internet Infrastructure Coalition:

The i2Coalition (Internet Infrastructure Coalition) ensures that those who build the infrastructure of the Internet have a voice in public policy. We are the leading voice for web hosting companies, data centers, domain registrars and registries, cloud infrastructure providers, managed services providers, and related tech. We protect innovation and the continued growth of the Internet’s infrastructure, which are essential to the global economy.

It has a site called VPNs at Risk, and a new report of the same name, which it says is “A comprehensive, content-neutral look at the technical and human impact of proposals affecting Virtual Private Networks.” It is a good introduction to the entire field, providing an approachable explanation of the technology that lies behind VPNs, as well as a useful survey of VPN regulations around the world, including those in India, United Kingdom, Pakistan, France, Iran, and Russia. It points out that there is a need for a broader conversation, since the questions raised by VPNs are not unique to that field:

Similar debates increasingly surround encryption, cloud computing, hosting, domain name systems, artificial intelligence, digital identity, and other technologies that provide general-purpose capabilities upon which many different users and services depend.

The rapid development and adoption of artificial intelligence make this broader conversation more urgent. As more consequential activities depend on connected systems, strong encryption, secure networking, and trustworthy Internet infrastructure become increasingly important. Policies that weaken these foundations can create vulnerabilities that extend well beyond their immediate targets. Addressing emerging risks should strengthen the infrastructure on which people and organizations depend, rather than compromise the tools that protect it.

an EU-wide system of anti-piracy injunctions – requiring providers to block access to websites and servers containing copyright-infringing content. Such a system risks turning providers of virtual private networks (VPNs) into watchdogs that have to filter traffic, undermining their core privacy-protecting function.

The DisCo article makes an important point:

In practice, pirates can quickly circumvent such measures, meaning that injunctions harm users’ privacy without delivering lasting results. Yet the blocking system remains under consideration for the Commission’s Copyright Package, due in the second quarter of 2027.

It’s time for EU policy- and decision-makers to commit unequivocally to preserving strong privacy protections and encryption, to focus anti-piracy enforcement on services that host illegal content and also have the ability to remove it, and to maintain a predictable regulatory environment for trusted VPN providers.

That certainly makes sense, but sense has never been much in evidence in the copyright world, which is driven by emotion and lobbying. Instead, we can probably expect increasingly strident calls for VPNs to be “reined in” in order to protect copyright – and the children, of course…

items.title: Microsoft Declares 'Code Red' After Historic Outage
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Microsoft has declared a "Code Red" initiative to overhaul its engineering and crisis response practices following a 24-hour outage on November 12-13 that disrupted governments, financial firms and airlines worldwide, according to internal memos reviewed by Reuters. Never before had so many customers been without email for so long, said M365 Core President Jason Henderson. "Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team," Henderson added. From the report: Amanda Silver, Microsoft's corporate vice president overseeing M365 Core and Work IQ, the company's workplace intelligence platform for AI agents, said in a separate memo on Monday that engineers had to work through a "fog of war" as the outage unfolded. Despite deploying top engineering personnel, responders exchanged more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats and struggled to maintain a cohesive picture of hypotheses and decisions because diagnostic data was scattered across fragmented internal tracking systems, Silver said.
 
[...] As part of the Code Red, a high-priority mobilization reserved for critical crises, Silver outlined five workstreams focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning and faster recovery mechanisms. Microsoft set a target of achieving worldwide resolution within an hour during future incidents and plans to deploy AI agents to help engineers diagnose system health data more quickly. Henderson said he would hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team, which oversees the engineering group responsible for underlying Microsoft 365 services, to track actions stemming from the outage, along with weekly reviews. The company spokesperson said Microsoft is committed not only to resolving issues when they occur, but to doing everything possible to prevent future disruptions.
 
"Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday," Henderson said, adding that he had conducted an extensive review of the broader organizational and structural issues that allowed the failures to occur. In another memo earlier this month reviewed by Reuters, Henderson said "urgent patches to our M365 Core services" took too long to deploy worldwide. "In a separate recent incident, an urgent production fix took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. For our most urgent security issues, we need to get from detection to safe worldwide deployment in an hour. Needless to say, we aren't here yet," he wrote.

items.title: Students Detained At Gunpoint After AI Says Their Bag Of Chips Is A Gun File Federal Lawsuit
items.author: Tim Cushing
items.content:
We covered the originating story almost exactly a year ago. That makes sense, because if you want to sue someone for rights violations, you almost always need to file that lawsuit prior to its 365-day expiration.

A year ago, there was a bit of an AI arms race between two companies who claimed adding their AI-enhanced cameras (or simply applying their algorithms to existing cameras) would be a game-changer when it came to school shootings. But neither of the companies got it right.

Evolv was generating tons of false positives in schools in which it had been deployed. Rather than make security easier for schools, schools were finding themselves forced to engage in far more in-person searches of inbound students, thanks to the tech deciding nearly student be carrying a gun.

“Today was probably the least safe day,” one principal observed the day scanners were deployed at her school, because the machines were triggering false alarms and requiring manual searches on “almost every child as they walked through” monopolizing the attention of safety officers who would otherwise be monitoring the halls and other entrances.

When asked about this, Evolv blamed the messenger. First, it claimed discussion of these failures “endangered” both students and educators. It also pulled publicly-available documentation of its tech from its website following this exposure of its failure, again pretending that anyone questioning the tech (or simply seeking more info) similarly “endangered” kids and teachers.

Omnilert is another major player in this space. Unlike Evolv’s apparently faulty body scanners that require students to walk through them before being searched by unpaid (at least by Evolv) human backstops, Omnilert uses AI to detect guns via analysis of camera images.

Omnilert soon proved itself to be equally incapable/infamous. Its public profile was raised after the tech to detect a gun carried by a student who killed one student and injured another before (self)-tapping out by turning the (undetected) gun on himself.

Adding insult to an un-prevented school shooting, Omnilert dug deeper, declaring a bag of Doritos carried by a student to be a gun. Multiple students were held at gunpoint during this investigation prompted by a rather egregious false positive. The Baltimore, Maryland students were accosted at gunpoint by a number of officers who were all carrying (and aiming) guns no human would mistake for a bag of Doritos. The students were handcuffed and held at gunpoint until further investigation revealed the MacGuffin was actually just a bag of Doritos.

Omnilert apologized, but did so in a way meant to shift blame from itself and its tech and to everyone else who was expected to act (perhaps violently!) every time its software cranked out a false positive.

Omnilert, the company that operates the AI gun detection system, expressed regret over the incident and emphasized that its system is designed to identify a possible threat and elevate it to human review.

“While the object was later determined not to be a firearm, the process functioned as intended: to prioritize safety and awareness through rapid human verification,” the company added.

That is some wild shit right there. When I think “human review,” I tend to think of employees of the tech provider doing some further inspection and providing a second opinion if things don’t seem to add up. “Human review” of potential false positives should be nothing more than scrambling a bunch of cops to the area, while feeding them no more information than the computer equivalent of “BRO SAW A GUN.” That’s the sort of thing that gets people killed.

Fortunately, these students managed to survive this encounter — one that was backstopped by “human review” that apparently involved not a single employee of Omnilert, but plenty of public servants who had real guns of their own. Once again, the private sector is perfectly happy to profit from its faulty tech. And it’s certainly not going to spend any money of its own on “human review,” not when it can outsource it to public employees and let the public pay (literally and otherwise) for any damage resulting from false positives.

Four current and former students at a Maryland high school have filed a lawsuit a year after armed police detained them, prompted by an AI alert that mistook a bag of Doritos for a gun, in an incident that left them “fearing for their lives”.

The plaintiffs sued Omnilert, the company behind the AI gun-detection system, Baltimore county police, the board of education, individual officers and the school principal, alleging unlawful detention and search because of technological and human errors.

The lawsuit itself contains a number of alarming details, including the sad fact that the officers distrusted Omnilert’s alerts, but still felt compelled to respond to them anyway.

The encounter was terrifying and life-threatening. With armed police encircling them for no apparent reason, each student feared for his life and the lives of his friends.

The officers’ search of the students turned up nothing. Only after the search did one of the officers reveal why they had been dispatched: “it’s the Omnilert.”

The officers on the scene knew OGD [Omnilert Gun Detect] was unreliable. One told the students that “AI is not the best.” Another muttered “stupid AI cameras” and “fucking Omnilerts.” Yet officers relied on the Alert to initiate this painful encounter with the students.

Worse, a “human review” did take place. Two school administrators who received the alert canceled it within two minutes of receiving it, having determined it showed nothing more than a student holding a bag of chips. Another “alert” was automatically generated by Omnilert, informing other school administrators (along with the police officers) that the “alert” had been canceled.

That should have been the end of it, but the principal of the school, Kate Smith, decided well after the original notification (and cancellation) that cops needed to go out and accost the chip-eating students.

But Defendant Catherine “Kate” SMITH, principal of Kenwood High School, never acknowledged the Alert’s cancelation or took any steps to verify whether the Alert remained active.

Instead, more than ten minutes after the Alert was canceled, Defendant SMITH viewed the text message containing the OGD Alert, opened the website linked in the text message, took a screenshot of the video footage of Taki holding the chip bag from that website, and sent the screenshot to School Resource Officer (“SRO”) John Douglas on his personal cell phone. SRO Douglas then forwarded the screenshot to BCoPD, prompting an armed police response.

A ten-minute delay in response is its own form of negligence, especially when Omnilert is expecting school administrators to backstop its AI. The principal obviously felt the (apparently innocuous) footage demanded a police response, but couldn’t be bothered to care until well after other, far more responsive school administrators had already responded to the alert.

Then, because the alert had been canceled, she was forced to screenshot the footage and manually send it to the school’s SRO to provoke an (extremely belated) police response to her message.

Finally, a few hours later, she decided to do a bit of lol’ing about the students she subjected a situation that easily could have turned deadly (for the students).

If you can’t see or read the embed, it’s a text message sent to other school administrators by Principal Kate Smith that reads:

Yep, that’s a principal laughing because the guns-out interaction she had personally provoked found nothing more than some students in possession of a bag of chips — a message punctuated by the “crying laughing emoji” which indicates (if you’re somehow not familiar) that the whole incident made the principal laugh so hard she produced tears of joy.

The footage captured by the school’s cameras clearly shows Taki holding (and eating from) a bag of chips. While you could grab a couple of frames here and there that might show some partially obscured metallic glints that could conceivably be to be a gun, the principal had access to the footage and could have seen the same thing we all can see here:

But instead of watching this, she chose to send images deprived of their context to the school resource officer, apparently in the sincere hope of provoking a police response. This decision seems at best to be deliberately negligent. At worst, it looks dangerously malicious. And when the cops showed up and miraculously managed to defuse the situation on their own, she laughed about it.

Vibes-wise, I think only the principal and school resource officer should be held personally accountable for this outcome. The law says otherwise, which means every defendant is fair game until a judge says otherwise. But what’s clearly demonstrated here — all rights aside — is that Principal Smith can’t be trusted to run a school, not if she’s carelessly (or callously) willing to endanger her own students.

items.title: Mayo Clinic To Give Appointment Workers 5 Paid Minutes a Day To Boot Up Computers
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Mayo Clinic has agreed to pay more than $906,000 in back wages to employees who schedule patient appointments. An investigation by Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison found that employees were performing unpaid work before and after their shifts, including time spent booting up computers and finishing patient calls. Under the settlement (PDF), Mayo will stop rounding employees' work hours and give them five paid minutes at the start of each shift to boot up their computers. CBS News reports: In a statement, Mayo Clinic said it reached the agreement to resolve concerns about "certain timekeeping practices" involving a group of the specialists. The clinic said it doesn't agree with the attorney general's position but decided that a resolution in which money went to its staff, rather than to defense fees, was preferable. Mayo said it is committed to paying employees accurately and appropriately and reviews its compensation policies regularly. Neither the announcement nor the statement says how many workers are covered or how far back the unpaid time goes.

items.title: I’ve Been Under A Rock. Why Is TikTok A National Security Threat, But Jensen Huang Is Fine?
items.author: Mike Masnick
items.content:
Hello, I have been living under a rock for the last twelve years. Can you help me understand the United States’ current views on tech policy and foreign affairs?

Oh boy. You’ve missed a lot. Okay, here in the second Donald Trump administration, China is clearly our biggest enemy and threat. Indeed, it’s such a huge threat that a bipartisan group of folks got together during the Biden administration (which happened between the two Trump administrations) to ban the Chinese social media site TikTok.

Oh wow. What is this TikTok anyway? Was it being used by the Chinese to conduct surveillance on Americans?

Not that anyone has ever been able to prove! It’s an app used by teens to share quick videos of themselves dancing. And sometimes they comment on the news.

Wait. And this is a problem?

Yes! As Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said while negotiating the forced sale of TikTok to US interests, the US is “not willing to sacrifice national security interests for a social media app.” Indeed, back when he was a Senator introducing one of the bills to ban TikTok if it stayed Chinese-owned, now-Secretary of State Marco Rubio made it quite clear: “We know it answers to the People’s Republic of China. There is no more time to waste on meaningless negotiations with a CCP-puppet company. It is time to ban Beijing-controlled TikTok for good.”

Wow. China must really be a serious threat to American tech interests. I assume we’re also banning the sale of our top-line semiconductors to China?

Well, about that… technically, we are banning the most sophisticated GPUs (necessary for building advanced artificial intelligence systems) to China, but Trump keeps allowing the leading GPU company, Nvidia, to sell its GPUs to China.

I assume they’re pretty careful about who those go to, though?

That’s crazy! Has he been arrested?

They… rehired him? The President? Called into a board meeting?

Oh yes. That’s how we do business in the US these days. The President considers it his duty to help rich cheating oligarchs who say nice things about him.

But does this mean he was illegally funneling strategically important technology to “our biggest enemy” at a time when we cannot “sacrifice national security”?

That’s cute. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says it’s no big deal because the chips weren’t going to the Chinese military, just to companies that work with the Chinese military — companies like Alibaba, which he described as mostly a social media company.

Isn’t he the same guy who said he wasn’t willing to sacrifice national security over a social media app? And didn’t Rubio say that TikTok answers to the People’s Republic of China? Would Alibaba do that too?

Sorry, were you expecting consistency? I guess now is the point I should mention that Jensen Huang also has been a prolific contributor to various Donald Trump extravagances, which appears to have bought him quite a lot of goodwill.

Surely someone in the administration is keeping an eye on this?

Well, yes, that’s the job of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is under fire for helping Huang and Nvidia sell more chips to China (did I mention the firm Lutnick ran for years, which is now run by his sons, has extensive ties to Nvidia?)

Wait, how is he still a cabinet member?

Actually, that’s a funny story! When Trump reportedly considered firing him over his ties to deceased underage sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein (also formerly Trump’s best friend), Lutnick donated $25 million to Trump’s Presidential library, which Trump asked Lutnick for directly. Indeed, it’s been reported that Trump brags that the only reason he keeps Lutnick around is the money he donated.

That all seems unbelievable. Doesn’t the US have laws to stop this kind of threat from foreign adversaries trying to corruptly influence our important tech supply chains?

Yes, but these days we only use them to threaten American companies that don’t allow the Fox News weekend anchor Trump put in charge of the Pentagon to use their AI services to launch autonomous attacks on brown people. That’s considered a “supply chain risk.” Having sex with (alleged) Chinese spies and blowing past export restrictions to ship our most powerful GPUs to China is just the cost of keeping the stock market artificially inflated.

Doesn’t that seem way more risky?

Sure, but risk isn’t really the point. It’s all part of Donald Trump’s rejection of capitalism, in favor of state control over industry, a la China.

Wait, the Republican Party now supports state control of businesses?

Not well. Democrats swept Congress in record-breaking ways (not to mention many other races around the country) even after Elon Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars trying to get Republicans elected.

Elon Musk? The electric car guy? I would have thought he was a liberal darling for pushing alternative energy?

So, to summarize, we tried banning the Chinese social media dancing app for “national security” reasons and punishing an American AI company because it won’t let the US indiscriminately use AI to kill people… but at the same time the President and his cabinet are interfering in private company governance to allow the guy who slept with an (alleged) Chinese spy and dodged export controls to give powerful computer chips to our biggest enemy, China, while the electric car guy is freely able to fiddle with satellite technology to prevent an American ally from defending itself against another enemy of the US, Russia?

Yeah, that’s pretty much the deal. I guess now is when I should mention that Donald Trump also is deeply invested in Nvidia to the tune of tens of millions of dollars, so he’s profiting from this mess. And, also that he called Russian leader Vladimir Putin his friend, even as Putin continues waging war on Ukraine and has spent decades working against the United States and its allies.

I’m going back under the rock.

Leave me alone! This timeline is ridiculous!

items.title: Google's Customized AI TV Channel, Starring You
items.author: Jason Koebler
items.content:
We promise 404 Media will never constantly generate customized AI newsletters for you. You'll get our flawed human tastes! And like it! (Hopefully)

Google has filed for a patent that would use the information it knows about you to create an AI-generated TV channel full of personalized “shows” starring you and featuring customized advertisements. The patent is the latest signal of the AI video endgame: endless highly specific, customized content that is automatically generated based on the wealth of data companies and advertisers collect about you.

Tech companies regularly file for patents that they don’t end up actually putting into real products, but this one, called “creating a channel of video experiences tailored to a user,” describes a system that many AI companies have been clearly trying to build. It imagines something called “My Channel,” which would be filled with AI content generated based on demographic data, their video watch history (presumably from YouTube), and other information it knows about the user. It would then make “the user as the protagonist for the whole video.” The patent was first noticed by Patentlyze, a news site that tracks tech company patents, who shared it with 404 Media.

“You are a customized video generating model. Generate a customized video for a user where the user will play the protagonist,” a hypothetical LLM prompt in the patent reads. “The generated customized video includes characteristics based on the <user_profile>. The generated customized video follows the style and format of the <top_ watches> of the user. The generated customized video sticks to the <preferred_genres> of the user but the narrative for the generated customized video is customized. The <top watches> and <preferred _genres> parameters are ordered from more preferred to less preferred.”

It suggests that the channel would be connected to an “advertising server,” and that advertisements would be inserted into the customized AI content: “an advertising stitcher included in the advertising server generates an updated customized media content item by inserting at least one advertisement into the customized media content item,” it says.

The patent imagines, for example, “a crime/comedy caper,” “a fun romantic comedy,” “a sci-fi adventure,” and “an action/thriller experience” with a viewer named “John” as the protagonist. Another prompt included in the patent suggests that someone who had recently watched cricket highlights of a “Player 1” might then be served a similar video “that incorporates elements of the Cricket World Cup and Player 1’s recent performance. Perhaps [user_name] could be cheering for India in the stands or interacting with Player 1 in some way.”

The notable thing about this patent is that it is barely an evolution of what is already happening on social media and what is beginning to happen on streaming free TV channels on services like Samsung TV Plus and TCLtv+.

The people generating AI slop on social media are making incredibly specific content because they know that social media algorithms will be highly effective at filtering people there. Meta is already allowing advertisers to use AI to generate many slightly different versions of an advertisement; its targeting AI then automatically shows them to users who are most likely to react to a specific version of an ad. As I’ve previously reported, TCL has been experimenting with AI-generated content on its streaming free TV channels, and, even without AI-generated content, free streaming TV channels have gotten incredibly specific. It is now possible, for example, to watch reruns of individual shows 24/7/365.

AI boosters have long been saying the future of entertainment is allowing anyone to generate their own TV shows, or to generate “new” episodes of existing properties. An always-on, autogenerating, customized AI TV channel isn’t far off from that idea.

As I’ve previously argued, the future that tech companies envision is one in which we are somehow even more siloed than we are now. They imagine a world in which everyone lives in their own reality and watches their own, customized content, which is a world in which big, unifying pieces of media are harder to make and are few and far between. The Google patent comes on the heels of a Microsoft patent that describes a system that alters spoken words (and the person’s lips) in live video, thereby distorting reality.

University Approves Nuclear Weapons Data Center, Township Vows to Fight OnLast week, the University of Michigan’s board of regents approved the construction of a $1.25 billion data center that will power American nuclear weapons research. The regents voted 7 - 1 in a public meeting on November 19 to move forward with the project despite widespread opposition from faculty, staff, and the residents of Ypsilanti Township, Michigan where the data center will operate. A few hours after the vote, the leaders and citizens of the Township gathered to discuss how to stop it.

University of Michigan Mailer Promises Its Data Center Isn’t Really a Data Center:And, related, over the past month, the University of Michigan sent postcards and pamphlets to people in Michigan telling them its new data center is “NOT a commercial data center” and is, instead, a “research computing center.” According to one of the postcards viewed by 404 Media, the University’s data center will “advance breakthrough research in medicine, clean energy, cybersecurity, and engineering,” and "accelerate discoveries like new drug therapies and cancer treatments that improve people’s lives.” The University's postcard also promised to create 300 “high-quality union jobs during development” and “preserve approximately 80% of the 124-acre property as green space.”

The biggest story in the tech world is, once again, Nvidia and the Jensen Huang scandal. Outside of mentioning it in this newsletter, we haven’t really been covering this. The main reason is that these are one of the few types of stories that we’re not really set up to do. Nvidia is technically the most valuable company on the planet, and so other bigger news outlets have a bunch of reporters who are dedicated to covering just Nvidia. When a scandal like this breaks, they throw entire news teams at it. It just doesn’t really make sense for us to try to compete with our smaller team. The New York Times, Bloomberg, The Information, and the Wall Street Journal (and lots of other outlets) are all over this. It does feel bad to more or less sit out such a big news story, and it’s not that we don’t think this scandal is important. It’s just that we are usually trying to break new ground, and it’s hard to do that when hundreds of other reporters are laser focused on the same scandal. We reserve the right to jump in at any time, especially with a reported take or something like this. I do think it’s depressing that this has become a culture war thing, and an opportunity for Silicon Valley VCs and billionaires to do class solidarity and try to show that there should be no consequences whatsoever for bad behaving CEOs. I think the Trump and essentially stock market by blackmail aspect of it all is quite worrisome, too. Huang’s return raises all sorts of national security concerns, corruption concerns, and questions about how (much more) subservient Huang will be to Trump now that he’s done him a massive favor. I also found this exchange to be upsetting on many levels. Also, this post from Balaji, one of the worst to ever do it, is wildly deranged and will probably make your blood boil. Anyways, that’s enough of that for the moment. Here’s what else is going on.

items.title: University of Michigan Mailer Promises Its Data Center Isn’t Really a Data Center
items.author: Matthew Gault
items.content:
Over the past month, the University of Michigan sent postcards and pamphlets to people in Michigan telling them its new data center is “NOT a commercial data center” and is, instead, a “research computing center.”

According to one of the postcards viewed by 404 Media, the University’s data center will “advance breakthrough research in medicine, clean energy, cybersecurity, and engineering,” and "accelerate discoveries like new drug therapies and cancer treatments that improve people’s lives.” The University's postcard also promised to create 300 “high-quality union jobs during development” and “preserve approximately 80% of the 124-acre property as green space.”

One of U of M’s mailers said the building will not operate as a commercial data center. “This facility will not support streaming, entertainment, social media, or e-commerce,” it said. It also said the facility will not “burden the local community with the cost of its energy or water use, drain resources from the local community or raise utility rates,” or “create smoke, odors, or significant noise.”

The University it’s not sure how much water the data center will use but that it could be as much as 650,000 gallons a day. It also said it’s “evaluating several cooling techniques to identify the most efficient approach,” a process that “includes continued evaluation of reclaimed wastewater for cooling, which would significantly reduce demand on municipal potable water supply systems.”

In April, the Township’s utilities authority on delivering water to data center projects while it studied how they might impact the community’s water supply. In response, U of M sent a letter to the Township utility board . 

Concerned Township residents have spent the past year strategizing with community leaders about how to delay or stop construction. The Township’s anger caught U of M off guard and it attempted to address community concerns in . It hasn’t gone well.

The pamphlet attempted to contextualize the data center’s place in America’s nuclear weapons research. “It would not involve nuclear weapons manufacturing, physical weapons testing, or the storage of hazardous nuclear materials,” the pamphlet said. But it would help “improve cybersecurity practices to safely manage existing nuclear material out of state.” In January, LANL confirmed its portion of the data center would be used for nuclear weapons research.

U of M did not return 404 Media’s request for comment.

On November 19, the board of regents of development for the data center in a . The same night, Ypsilanti Township hosted a panel discussion about the data center where its leaders promised to continue to fight. “We have a number of strategies right now that we’re going to be pursuing,” Township attorney Douglas Winters said at the panel. “We believe that U of M has gone far afield when it comes to the constitutional autonomy which they have enjoyed by virtue of being a university.”

Ellison’s gushing, over the top praise not only insisted it’s an honor to have a white supremacist investing in the new media conglomerate, but Ellison also goes out of his way to continue to prop up Elon Musk’s phony supergenius engineer mythology:

“So look, I have so much admiration and respect for Elon. I mean, I don’t know if you saw recently, but literally watching, you know, [SpaceX’s] Starship, it’s a marvel…. I mean, he is both the [Nikola] Tesla and [Thomas] Edison… He is, from my perspective, the greatest entrepreneur of our time, and he doesn’t invest in a lot of companies.”

“So to have his vote of confidence and to have him as a shareholder is an honor and a privilege. And if there was any opportunity to be able to collaborate with him in the future… [which] is the appropriate opportunity in the future, we’d be thrilled to do so. But there’s nothing [right now].”

The idea that Musk sits around in his overalls designing rocket engines was a press and business community mythology for the better part of the last twenty years. In reality, Musk is an opportunist who lucked into PayPal money, then used his fortune to opportunistically glom on to actual innovators and take singular credit for their ideas. While endlessly cutting corners and breaking the law.

While that ultimately did help goose interest in space travel resulting in some actual innovation at SpaceX, anybody who, in 2026, is still comparing Musk to actual inventors like Tesla is telling you they’re an intellectual toddler.

At that point it’s probably a good time to thank California AG Rob Bonta and outgoing Governor Gavin Newsom, who thought they were “helping Hollywood” by pressuring state AGs to scuttle their lawsuit against the pointless and disastrous deal. items.title: Russia May Launch Nuclear Weapon Into Orbit As Soon As Next Month

items.content:
Western intelligence agencies reportedly believe Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite into orbit as early as December, "suggesting the country's development of a satellite-killing weapon of mass destruction is more advanced than previously thought," reports Ars Technica, citing German media reports. Such a launch would violate the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, while a detonation could create radiation belts that damage satellites for years. From the report: The orbiting nuclear weapon would threaten thousands of satellites in low-Earth orbit, including military and commercial communications networks like Starshield and Starlink. A nuclear-armed satellite would also put at risk Western military surveillance satellites and human spaceflight platforms like the International Space Station. A nuclear detonation in orbit would be indiscriminate, also knocking out Russia's own spacecraft and Chinese satellites.
 
Reporting from three German news outlets -- public broadcasters NDR and WDR and the Munich-based newspaper Suddeutsche Zeitung -- indicates Russia's launch of a nuclear-armed satellite could be imminent. The report says Western intelligence agencies, including the German Armed Forces and Federal Intelligence Service, believe Russia is preparing to deploy the weapon in space this year. Several NATO countries have exchanged their findings on the matter.
 
The nuclear-armed satellite, designated Sputnik-S, has been in storage in the greater Moscow area for years, the German news report said. German Space Command believes the satellite could be launched as early as December. Once in orbit, a nuclear weapon could loiter for months or years, ready for detonation on the command of Russian military forces. The Kremlin dismissed the report. "Given the number of qualifiers like 'allegedly' and 'possibly' -- not to mention the fact that the claims are attributed to some unspecified source -- they are hardly worth taking seriously," said Dmitry Peskov, spokesperson for Russian President Vladimir Putin.

items.title: Beaver’s Mini Mart Files Motion To Dismiss That Is A Masterful Takedown Of Buc-ee’s Bullshit
items.author: Timothy Geigner
items.content:
It’s been a while since we checked in on the whole Buc-ee’s vs. Beaver’s Mini Mart saga. It was in the wake of John Oliver focusing on Buc-ee’s trademark bullying ways on that Buc-ee’s decided to sue a tiny convenience store in Ohio for trademark infringement. The original suit, like many Buc-ee’s suits before it, keyed in on the cartoon beaver mascot that Beaver’s Mini Mart featured on its storefront signage, along with the name “Beaver’s,” since Buc-ee’s has a trademark on that term as well. The problems were obvious: the cartoons don’t look anything like Buc-ee’s beaver mascot, and the town where the mini mart resides is in Beavercreek, which is where it got its name.

Buc-ee’s ended up amending its complaint afterwards. In the second version, it doesn’t allege infringement due to the beaver mascot, though it still includes plenty of pictures of its own beaver cartoon mascot to imply it’s a problem. Instead, it focuses only on the mart’s use of “beaver” in its name, and then draws all kinds of conclusions as to why it’s all a problem without alleging any real facts.

The parent organization of Beaver’s Mini Mart, Hanes Road Carryout, Inc., just filed for a motion to dismiss and its a masterful takedown that points out, repeatedly, that all the lawsuit does is reach a bunch of conclusions without providing a scintilla of actual evidence for anything at all.

Attorneys for Hanes Road Carryout, which operates the store on Hanes Road in Beavercreek, filed the motion Monday in U.S. District Court in Dayton. It argues the businesses make very different impressions: Beaver’s Mini Mart is a small neighborhood convenience store, while Buc-ee’s presents itself as a large, highway-oriented travel center. The motion also says Buc-ee’s has not identified a customer who was actually confused or explained how the businesses reach customers through the same marketing channels.

The motion also disputes Buc-ee’s claim that Hanes Road deliberately copied its brand. Hanes Road points to a Beavercreek sign permit record from 2019 and argues the store was using the “Beaver’s” name before Buc-ee’s says it first used its registered “BEAVER’S” mark in commerce.

It does all of that, yes, but you really have to be witness to the layers of snark delivered in the motion. Take this paragraph on how speculative Buc-ee’s concerns are, given that both businesses have existed for several years now.

Despite Defendant’s use of Beaver’s Mini Mart since at least 2019 (a matter of public record that Buc-ee’s acknowledges now), Plaintiff failed to allege a single inquiry, transaction, or communication involving a confused consumer. Nor has Plaintiff identified common advertising, shared promotional methods, or overlapping marketing channels where consumers encounter the marks. Instead, despite six plus years of Defendant’s operation as Beaver’s Mini Mart, Plaintiff speculates that consumers might associate Defendant’s convenience store with Buc-ee’s.

Or this section, which defends the mini mart against Buc-ee’s claims that the supposed infringement was done intentionally and in bad faith.

Despite Hanes Road’s simplicity and long existence, Buc-ee’s alleges, on information and belief, that Hanes Road acted deliberately, willfully, intentionally, or in bad faith, with knowledge of Buc-ee’s rights and an intent to cause confusion and trade upon Buc-ee’s goodwill. Am. Compl. (emphasis added). Plaintiff does not allege when or how Hanes Road learned of Buc-ee’s marks, a previous relationship with Buc-ee’s, access to Buc-ee’s branding, copying instructions, progressive alteration of Hanes Road’s branding, or any communication reflecting imitation. Hanes Road would have to have been clairvoyant to have intentionally infringed on the trademark; reasonable inferences from the pleaded facts do not establish intent.

Even so, Buc-ee’s labels Hanes Road’s conduct as willful and in bad faith, characterizes the matter as exceptional, and seeks attorneys’ fees and enhanced monetary relief and Prayer for Relief. Buc-ee’s allegations about intent and willfulness are implausible given that Hanes Road undeniably began using the name and sign before Buc-ee’s (and years before Buc-ee’s came to Ohio).

In more common parlance: hey, Buc-ee’s is just making shit up!

And that’s indeed what is happening here. The Beaver’s Mini Mart is in no way a threat to Buc-ee’s and its plans to expand in Ohio. There is no public confusion on offer here. If there were, Buc-ee’s would have included it in their lawsuit, as that would make the case much closer to a slam dunk.

No, Buc-ee’s is trademark bullying because it’s a trademark bully. Entities like this just can’t help themselves. But it sure would be nice if the court could do the nation a kindness and clap back by dismissing this turd of a trademark suit.

items.title: Outage Chaos: When Tech Is Too Big To Fail
items.author: Rory Mir
items.content:
Outages happen, but we deserve a resilient internet where no one outage at one company can put people at risk and disrupt the global economy. We can only get there by addressing an over-reliance on a few cloud monopolists through effective antitrust laws and interoperability requirements.

Service outages, like we’ve seen recently at Microsoft, Apple, banks, courts, airlines, and elsewhere, can be more than an annoying hurdle. Losing a vital service due to an error can cause the same impacts as a government-ordered internet shutdown—people losing access to vital information and lines of communication.  As usual, the greatest harms are faced by people on the margins globally.

There’s not much hope in companies out-nerding these issues either. Technical errors will always exist, whether it’s a bug, negligence from an administrator, or a malicious attack. The problem is an over-reliance on any one company or system when these inevitable outages occur. It’s a matter of public safety and economic stability that policymakers mitigate the impact of these disruptions before they occur. 

In order to do so, we must ensure antitrust prevents providers of key technical systems from becoming too big to fail.

The harms inflicted by tech monopolies go beyond monetary costs to the end user. In fact, monopolists can often offer lower prices, or even offer free services, thanks to their greater scale and incentive to shut out competitors using free-flowing investment capital. The problem is this puts a few tech companies in a position of incredible influence. The true cost is a loss of control when our private data, access to knowledge, and free expression all become mediated by tools owned by a handful of billionaires.

This isn’t just a bad deal for us as individuals. Losing diversity in our digital infrastructure creates a less stable and less resilient internet for everyone. When everything from daily tasks to national security is reliant on a few digital monocultures, one mistake or exploit can cascade into an explosive impact. The risks multiply in the current investment climate, where financial markets reward companies that strip-mine redundancy and resiliency from critical systems. Even if you see the problem coming, an outage that hits clients, suppliers, collaborators or loved ones proves just as disruptive. We need to remove these chokepoints for good, which means a digital sovereignty movement that makes the web more free by design—not just importing existing levers of control into another nation’s borders.

Central to this effort must be undercutting platform control by fostering interoperability, i.e. when tools are made to be compatible among competitors. When this is done carefully, it’s not only easier to switch to better alternatives, we wind up with as it becomes more viable to compete or offer complementary tools alongside existing systems. 

This is what made systems like email great. You could choose your own apps and services, even using several simultaneously, and never lose touch with a contact. Early architects of the internet did not take reliable hosting for granted. Services were often on a machine a few rooms over, and needed to be prepared for the occasional interruption of service.

But in the age of hyperscalers and massive data centers, the infrastructure underlying the web isn’t owned by many scattered IT departments, it’s rented from a handful of “cloud” providers. These providers managed to scale up quickly and replace interoperability with walled gardens, enticing customers with lower costs while making it costly to leave and tightly controlling how services behave. Once in control, these platforms have every incentive to enshittify their services and devalue their workers, delivering an increasingly shoddy and restrictive service. 

This context makes building interoperability an act of defiance—often coming from the sweat of open source developers. These projects may be tolerated by monopolists in the short term, but can be one boardroom decision away from being broken entirely. A better internet means championing these creators through funding, liability protections, and requiring big players to cooperate. Here is what lawmakers should do:

Federal and state legislators should—

  • Defend competitive compatibility. Developers merely providing alternative interfaces for tools should be shielded from liability. In the U.S., that means explicit protections under DMCA, CFAA, and corporate Terms of Service agreements. These protections should cover shared protocols and APIs as well as automated content retrieval through scraping. 
  • Encourage interoperability. Lawmakers should force open key aspects of platform infrastructure by requiring big tech to support: (1) data portability, so users can move to a new service (2) back-end interoperability, to support more tools with competitive compatibility and (3) delegability, so people are not prevented from having code act on their behalf. So far, the Digital Markets Act in the EU has provided some positive examples of such legislation
  • In order to be sustainable, interoperable tools and standards cannot rely solely on corporate interest and volunteer labor. Programs like the EU Sovereign Tech Fund could help create viable alternatives within and beyond the borders of the EU.

Municipalities and institutions should—

  • Buy interoperable services. At any level, government agencies should set minimum interoperability requirements in procurement and hold a competitive bidding process to evaluate vendors’ privacy, security and lock-in risks. Agencies dependent on a sole provider, including through cooperative purchase agreements, are stuck with corporate price-gouging and even higher switching costs.
  • Fund Departments of Information Technology. Cloud services are often adopted to offset spending on IT professionals but, when these departments atrophy, institutions become even more reliant on the cloud providers. Maintaining in-house talent prevents this cycle of dependency and improves emergency responses to outages. 
  • Adopt a plus-one approach to public communications. Institutions shouldn’t force citizens into walled gardens just to access public communications. In addition to posts to corporate social media, government agencies should share the same information on an open protocol—whether it’s bluesky, the fediverse, or just an RSS feed.  By putting these in the open, more people will have access to urgent alerts and can create new useful tools.

Building a more resilient and democratic internet is possible, and many people are already hard at work doing just that. Above are some necessary steps to get corporate and government interests out of the way of rewilding the net with greater community and individual controls. The dream of the internet as a digital commons operating for the public good is not dead yet, and is worth fighting for.

items.title: Judge Berates ICE For Re-Arresting Migrants Released By Court Orders
items.author: Tim Cushing
items.content:
Apparently, the Trump administration felt its war on migrants just wasn’t cruel enough. In addition to sending ICE officers to green card/naturalization hearings to sweep up people trying to follow the legal path to citizenship, ICE continued to swiftly move detainees from detention center to detention center with the obvious desire to keep them separated from their due process rights. (And that’s on top of arbitrarily shipping people to whatever country will take them — a list that is made up mostly of cash-hungry, war-torn countries with long histories of human rights abuses.)

Since the courts have been less than cooperative, Trump — aided and abetted by resident migrant-hating ghoul Stephen Miller (who was recently elevated to official Chief of Staff) — has been doing anything it can to stay ahead of the 10,000+ (and counting!) federal court decisions finding in favor of migrants and their due process rights.

The administration has flooded the zone. While Trump obviously hoped this would allow his administration to bypass due process by simply giving the courts too much to handle, it has become clear this effort has overwhelmed his prosecutors and immigration-focused lawyers.

The only entity left with an appreciable amount of manpower is ICE. And since the administration can’t “win” its bigoted game of 1-D Candyland by playing by the rules, it has decided to do something that has never been done by this country since the (unfortunate) formation of ICE. ICE is now immediately re-arresting migrants who’ve been freed by federal court orders — something it has accomplished by sending ICE officers to courtrooms where the administration already knows it has lost.

But the day he was released wasn’t the day he would ultimately get his freedom.

“An ICE officer came and said, ‘Oh, I’ll escort you out,’” said Emmanuel. “[He] handed me my bag and said, ‘Ok, you’ve been released,’ and as soon as I stepped out one step, there were five ICE officers that were waiting outside in bulletproof vests and cameras and everything. And they grabbed me, and they said, ‘Oh, you’ve been re-arrested from that release.’”

When a court says your due process rights exist and you’re free to go, it doesn’t mean you’re only free until you run into the nearest masked ICE officers, now conveniently located immediately at courtroom exit doors.

Judge Sweeney ordered the ICE field office director handling this area to appear in court to answer her questions directly. The answers obviously didn’t satisfy the judge, as this court order [PDF] makes clear [emphasis in the original]. (h/t Kyle Cheney)

Certain legal principles—perhaps some that are more technical in nature—are known to trained lawyers. Yet many of these principles are obvious to every American. For instance, that certain freedoms are “not the government’s to take.” Stanford Daily Publ’g Corp. v. Rubio, No. 25–cv–06618–NW, — F. Supp. 3d —-, 2026 WL 2549090, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 28, 2026). This case concerns one such technical legal principle—what must a disobedient party do to be held in contempt—with one that is more obvious in nature—everyone is entitled to due process. This includes noncitizens residing in this country.

What’s absolutely depressing about this court order is how little the administration cares what the system of checks and balances has to say about its actions. Another plaintiff who was immediately re-arrested by ICE after being freed from detention by a federal court order is discussed here. The repetition of these events makes it impossible for ICE to pretend this isn’t its new standard operating procedure.

This status report arrived on November 3, 2026. In this report, Respondents stated that Mr. Quintero Alvarez was “released from immigration custody on October 27, 2026.” But there’s more: He was “immediately re-detained,” and at the time of the status report’s submission “remain[ed] in detention.” Just as these representations were unequivocal, so too was Respondents’ counsel’s representation that they would “not be submitting a brief that argue[d] that” Mr. Quintero Alvarez’s detention at the time was “lawful.” Ergo, his detention was unlawful.

The administration is still in the “fuck the courts” business — a business that was allegedly established by none other than a current Trump federal court appointee, Emil Bove.

The order goes on to note that the government didn’t even argue that the re-arrest and re-detention of Mr. Alvarez was lawful. In fact, Field Office Director Nichole Black simply agreed to the narrative provided by Alvarez. Alvarez was released by the court, given his personal possessions, and — as soon as he walked out to the lobby of the court (“into a public area”), ICE officers arrested him.

ICE Field Office Director Nichole Black offered up the Nuremberg Defense when questioned directly by Judge Sweeney:

In response to these questions, Ms. Black confirmed that she was instructed to rearrest habeas petitioners…

Black claimed the re-arrest program only targeted people “who had some type of ‘criminality'”. But she still admitted the re-arrest violated the court order releasing Alvarez, as well never offering any argument justifying this new policy, much less this re-arrest. So, the qualifications offered in Black’s modified “you know, the thing the Nazis said” defense ultimately don’t matter. And they don’t matter after Black admitted the “some type of criminality” used to re-arrest Alvarez was predicated on “inaccurate information.”

Black only dodges contempt charges because ICE to have abandoned this re-arrest activity shortly after the court’s first angry encounter earlier this month. (The judge will still be watching to see what happens going forward, since this narrative was presented in the form of sworn statements and testimony by ICE officials, which means they likely won’t get away with this a second time.) And since Alvarez is actually finally free to go (and has yet to be re-arrested by ICE), his case is over as well.

But Judge Sweeney lets both ICE, other courts, and the general public know ICE’s actions are so far out of bounds, it’s almost impossible to craft an order that isn’t just “What the fucking fuck?!” repeated for 15 pages.

Sometimes, behavior stuns and renders a listener speechless. In one turn of phrase, lost for words. To the extent any reader may be lost for words as to what ICE and Respondents did in this case and others in this judicial district like it—and the ridiculous nature of the justification for their behavior—turn to what the Supreme Court has said repeatedly over the course of our Nation’s history. “The government of the United States has been emphatically termed a government of laws and not of men.” State of Louisiana ex rel. Elliott v. Jumel, 107 U.S. 711, 743 (1883). “Our system of jurisprudence rests on the assumption that all individuals, whatever their position in government, are subject tofederal law.” Davis v. Passman, 442 U.S. 228, 246 (1979) (citation modified). “‘All men are equal before the law,’ ‘This is a government of laws and not of men,’ ‘No man is above the law,’ are all maxims showing the spirit in which Legislatures, executives and courtsare expected to make, execute and apply laws.” Truax v. Corrigan, 257 U.S. 312, 332 (1921). Any reader—and chief among them, Respondents—would do well to keep these binding statements in mind.

While history (and precedent) certainly makes it clear ICE is operating well outside what’s considered to be normal and acceptable in this country, I’m not so sure the Supreme Court would agree. That’s a real problem if ICE (especially now that Stephen Miller is now officially part of Trump’s Cabinet) decides to press the issue. While there may be no precedent supporting its current actions, the novelty of its grotesqueness might be all it needs to secure the blessing of a Supreme Court whose majority hasn’t met a novel Trump argument it doesn’t like.
