items.title: University Approves Nuclear Weapons Data Center, Township Vows to Fight On
items.author: Matthew Gault
items.content:
Last week, the University of Michigan’s board of regents approved the construction of a $1.25 billion data center that will power American nuclear weapons research. The regents voted 7 - 1 in a public meeting on November 19 to move forward with the project despite widespread opposition from faculty, staff, and the residents of Ypsilanti Township, Michigan where the data center will operate. A few hours after the vote, the leaders and citizens of the Township gathered to discuss how to stop it.

U of M and Los Alamos National Laboratories (LANL) first announced plans to build what the University then called an “AI research facility” in 2024. U of M now calls the project a “research computing center” and, if all goes to its plan, construction will begin on a 125,000 square foot facility in late 2027. The data center could expand to “no more than 300,000 square feet,” according to a .

During the regent’s meeting, faculty, staff, and members of the community shared their thoughts on the data center’s construction.

“It is widely promoted as the next step in furthering novel research taking place at this University. What is conveniently left out on flyers and pamphlets is that this is only part of the proposition, 10% in fact, the other 90% is being used by Los Alamos — a nuclear weapons developer,” a sophomore studying biochemistry told the board before the vote. “We already have three existing high tech data centers used for research. Why must we push forward with another one that is promoting nuclear warfare?”

An electrician from Ypsilanti Township, a representative of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW) union, supported the construction project. “This will create 300 plus jobs for our members, all local, [and] give back to the community,” he said. “IBEW is in favor of the data center, excuse me, ‘high compute research center.’”

People who attended the regent’s meeting to discuss other topics referenced the vote during their presentations. “You voted today to fund a $785 million data center project in Ypsilanti, much to the opposition of the residents of the area, acting against what many residents in the area are calling environmental racism. I think I can speak for many students when I say I am frankly appalled by this decision,” a student who was there to discuss carbon emissions said.

A library worker present to talk about how the University treats its workers invoked the data center. “I’m not sure I can confidently appeal to your sense of compassion around this. The officials and residents of Ypsi Township are saying ‘stop,’ saying ‘no,’ saying ‘this hurts.’ And you and others responsible for this nuclear weapons data center project have shown you don’t care about the basic issue of consent as you plow ahead,” he said.

Ypsilanti Township is at the tip of the spear in the new nuclear arms race.

Despite the opposition in the room, the regents approved the project. “It’s been very controversial [...] For me, this is all about an investment in the community and it’s an investment, in many different ways,” regent Denise Ilitch said just before the vote. “The community will be enhanced — they may not feel it now, some, but I venture to say that there will be much good that will come from this.”

Many in Ypsilanti Township disagree. After the regents voted, the leadership and residents of the Township gathered for a panel discussion about the data center. One of the speakers that night was Jay Coghlan, the executive director of Nuclear Watch of New Mexico, a watchdog group that tracks Los Alamos. “The data center issue here in Ypsilanti is unique in that it is the clearest example of the pending merger of AI and nuclear weapons, which doesn’t bode well,” Coghlan told 404 Media.

Coghlan told 404 Media that he shared the Township’s concerns about how the data center will use water and electricity but said he thinks its construction will have farther reaching consequences. “Our nation is transforming from the military-industrial complex that Eisenhower warned us about to a Silicon Valley-Pentagon-Wall Street complex that closely links economics, economic inequality, increasing militarism, and I dare say the rise of techno-fascism,” he said.

U of M has repeatedly said the data center will mostly be used to power medical breakthroughs and conduct cancer research, something it’s highlighted in flyers and pamphlets it’s mailed to people in the Township. LANL to the people of the community in September that promised it wouldn't build nuclear weapons in their backyard. 

“I'm going  ‘Duh, yeah, you're not going to bring plutonium to Ypsilanti in Michigan,” Coghlan said. “But I expect this data center to have a lot to do with the design of new nuclear weapons. So, in that way, Ypsilanti Township is at the tip of the spear in the new nuclear arms race.”

Coghlan  said he finds hope in the opposition to the project. “I’m very impressed by the intensity of opposition that I have witnessed. There seems to be a pretty widespread public awareness of the data center in Ypsilanti, Township.”

During the Township meeting on November 19, after the regents voted, Ypsilanti Township attorney Douglas Winters said he was mad. “What did we learn on November 3rd? Two weeks ago and two days, voters around this country loudly declared that they were sick and tired of government corruption. They were tired of secrecy. They were tired of abuse of power. They were tired of threats to democracy and the disregard of governmental accountability. And, importantly, they also said they were sick and tired of these data centers,” he said. “Somehow that message did not make it to Ann Arbor. That message did not make it to the board of regents.”

Winters and other leaders vowed to keep fighting the data center’s construction. In May, the community’s water authority voted to restrict new construction on infrastructure to data center projects while it conducts a review of their impact on the Township’s water supply. The University called the move “unlawfully discriminatory.” In August, the Township passed a six month moratorium on new electrical infrastructure, a move aimed at delaying the project.

But Huang’s exodus, while the legally correct move, was starting to seriously disrupt AI and data center investment markets, now bone-grafted to the U.S. economy. The threat of multiple investigations into Nvidia’s financing (and potential infiltration by the Chinese) was jeopardizing Nvidia’s role as the single most-important subsidizing mechanism keeping the AI bubble (and its circular financing) afloat.

“NVIDIA today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.”

Well cool, so glad that’s settled. To start, this is Nvidia openly saying they don’t care about Huang leveraging his authority to have sex with subordinates, something Nvidia employees will likely remember the next time they’re required to sit through workplace sensitivity and ethics training.

But more importantly, this is just foundationally from a legal standpoint. There’s been no meaningful investigation into Huang’s long relationship with alleged Chinese asset Alice Huang. They have absolutely no idea how compromised Huang’s devices or the Nvidia network is. Nor has anybody even really started digging into Nvidia’s alleged export ban violations or funny financials in Singapore.

But worry not! In its statement, Nvidia reiterates that they’ve set up a new commission tasked with making sure it is adhering to export controls and the law (read: there’s no need for pesky government inquiries or deep dives into our finances):

“As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.”

Despite numerous media outlets credulously insisting last week that the Trump SEC and DOJ were “investigating,” in a statement Donald made it very clear that won’t be happening:

How many Trump insiders do you think had early warnings of Huang’s reinstatement and profited off the resulting stock bump?

This is not how serious countries function, and this is a dangerous embarrassment. It does, however, speak to how desperate tech titans are to keep the AI industry’s circular financing afloat, which continues to cover up the fact that the lion’s share of large AI companies simply aren’t profitable, and that a massive amount of heavily-debt-addled data center investments likely won’t be completed leaving your retirement money likely holding the bag after the “market correction.”

This corrupt and embarrassing capitulation won’t prevent an AI bubble from popping longer term. And while neither Nvidia nor the Trump administration will be particularly incentivized to transparently get to the truth of what happened, a flood of investigations by a reconstituted Congress in the new year is likely to shed all sorts of interesting new details on the entire affair(s) anyway.

This is Nvidia very clearly putting the AI hype bubble (and the interests of the extraction class) above ethics, morality, and even national security. It’s utterly clownish, but it’s extremely on par for a country that’s being steadily hollowed out by unethical autocratic corruption.

items.title: Trump Is Said to Have Directed Effort to Reinstate Nvidia Chief
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
President Trump reportedly directed a behind-the-scenes effort to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO, enlisting Vice President JD Vance to secure assurances from federal officials that Huang was not facing criminal charges or considered a national security risk. According to The New York Times, the intervention came despite intelligence concerns surrounding Huang's alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese spy linked to an investigation into illegal Nvidia chip shipments to China. From the report: [...] Only a tiny handful of officials at the highest level of the government were aware of these conversations. On Sunday night, Nvidia's board told the administration that it would be announcing Mr. Huang's reinstatement on Monday morning before the markets opened. The announcement included a note about a new compliance committee, intended to offer public assurance that the company was taking seriously the investigation into the possible smuggling of advanced chips. Mr. Trump was said to have been thrilled that the plan to restore Mr. Huang was executed without any leaks.
 
In directing Mr. Vance to engage with Mr. Huang and his peers, Mr. Trump was turning to one of the members of his administration with the strongest relationships in Silicon Valley. The vice president is close to some of Mr. Huang's biggest supporters and admirers, such as David Sacks, the investor and co-chairman of the President's Council of Advisers on Science and Technology. Mr. Sacks previously served as Mr. Trump's key adviser on artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency issues.
 
On Monday morning, Mr. Trump rejoiced in Nvidia's action, saying on his social media website Truth Social that the company "made the correct and proper decision." The president explicitly connected the reinstatement of Mr. Huang to the health of the U.S. economy. "The Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy," Mr. Trump wrote.

items.title: YC Startup Working On 'Cost Per Kill' For Missiles
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: At 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote. Or drink. Or smoke. Or drive unsupervised. But he's not too young to win half a million dollars for his AI-guided-missile startup. In September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator's fall 2026 cohort. The startup accelerator counts companies like Airbnb, Stripe, DoorDash, and Reddit among its alumni; Dandzbergs is likely the youngest solo founder in its vaunted history. His startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a new class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts. "I think missiles are the coolest thing," Dandzbergs tells WIRED. "A lot of people that have found success in engineering early on have had a passion for blowing stuff up."
 
In conversation, Dandzbergs is poised and articulate. He talks about "attacking hard problems," breaking things down to "first principles," and how the Ukraine conflict has forever altered the theater of war -- a personal fixation, given his country's proximity to Russia. He projects an unassailable confidence in his own abilities. "He's a pretty exceptional person," says Harj Taggar, a YC partner assigned to mentor Dandzbergs. "I'm still somewhat in disbelief that we're talking about a 16-year-old." Dandzbergs has resolved to apply these unusual talents to figuring out how to optimize targeted killing. His startup's guiding ambition, according to its investor one-pager, is to bring down the "cost per kill." Dandzbergs hopes to demonstrate a prototype missile by December. Despite concerns about the ethical implications of autonomous weapons and his young age, he remains undeterred. "I want to be part of it. I want to move with the future of warfare," he says.
 
"Please don't say I'm sacrificing my childhood," says Dandzbergs. "This is the childhood I dreamed of."

items.title: Teens To Lawmakers: Excluding Us Isn’t The Same As Protecting Us
items.author: Mike Masnick
items.content:
For years and years now we’ve been pointing out that — contrary to popular opinion — the data just doesn’t support the idea that social media is inherently bad for teens. And yet, the media and politicians keep acting as if it’s inarguable. What the data does show is that a very small percentage of teens (somewhere around 3 to 4%) struggle with how much time they spend on social media. And often, social media isn’t the cause of that struggle. Those kids are frequently dealing with other challenges or mental health issues, lack adequate support or treatment, and turn to social media to fill the gap.

We’ve long argued that a better approach is to identify those teens and figure out how to get them actual help, while giving everyone else the tools and education (from both parents and teachers) to use the technology in age-appropriate ways.

And many kids seem to feel the same way. Yes, you can take this with a grain of salt given that Snap Inc. is the one publishing it, but a bunch of teen groups and youth safety councils have gotten together on an incredibly well-done open letter to politicians around the globe, telling them to stop experimenting on kids without talking to kids, and to stop rushing to just ban the tech.

The letter is from a bunch of groups, including ConnectSafely, Ditch The Label, NetSafe Youth Action Squad, Our Minds Matter, Project Rockit, Young Leaders for Active Citizenship, Youth Ki Awaaz, and Snap’s Global Councils for Digital Well-Being. That’s a big, global coalition of public interest groups driven by actual teens.

The letter makes a bunch of great points and is highly quotable.

We are teens from various organizations around the world. And, we are tired of watching adults debate our lives as if we are not in the room. 

This reminds me of a child internet safety event I went to a few years ago that opened with a panel of actual teenagers. It completely shifted the tone of everything that followed. So much of the discussion about kid safety online is driven by out of touch, technically clueless adults, doing the typical moral panic about “the kids these days and their newfangled way of communicating.”

Here, the kids call this out. They also don’t deny that the tech itself does have some issues that need fixing, but make it clear that simply banning kids from the tech does little to fix things:

Let’s be clear: teens did not create the current digital landscape. We did not design digital products. We did not write weak laws, delay reforms, ignore evidence, or treat our well-being as a talking point to be used only when politically convenient. And now, after years of adults failing to fix the real problems, a lot of leaders have landed on the same blunt and easy answer: take social media away from us. 

That is not leadership. That is surrender. 

It’s easier to ban than to build. It’s easier to blame technology and teenagers than to do the slower, harder work of actually fixing what is broken. That means real rules, real oversight, better digital literacy, safer product design, and more support for families and schools. It’s easier to announce a headline-grabbing restriction than to admit that politicians and adults themselves have helped create the vacuum they are now trying to fill with panic.

And now teens are paying the price. We are paying with our connections. With our communities. With our support systems. With our learning. With our creativity. With our joy. 

They also point out that — while adults dismissively insist that kids should just get off the internet — the reality is that the internet is now deeply integrated into their social lives and identity:

For many of us, social media is not just some extra, silly thing we could easily lose. Adults often talk about our “digital lives” like they are separate from our real ones. For us, they aren’t two different things. 

Social media is a big part of where life happens. It’s where we keep up with our friends across towns and time zones. It’s where we laugh after long days at school. It’s where we learn and discover new ideas, find role models, explore our identities, and access communities that may not exist for us offline. It’s where isolated teens find belonging. It’s where vulnerable teens sometimes find help. These are often marginalized or LGBTQ+ teens who can’t find community where they live, and are further hurt when prevented from making connections online. A study by the Born This Way Foundation found that 44% of LGBTQ+ youth feel “very safe” in online spaces compared to just 9% in-person. 

They point out that the bans don’t work — and drive the point home by asking how adults would feel if they were banned from the technology they use every day.

The reality is that vital age verification needed for these sorts of bans is difficult to implement, and teens are inherently tech-savvy. Driven by our desire to stay connected, many of us will naturally turn to VPN workarounds, alternative accounts, and unmonitored corners of the internet where there is even less oversight and even greater potential danger. 

To adults who dismiss our concerns as superficial, we ask: would you say the same thing about your group chats, your work messages, neighborhood groups, news feeds, or the people you speak to online every day? If connection matters for you, it matters for us, too. 

And they make the point I keep trying to make: there’s a better approach, and it involves actually teaching kids how to use the tech. A couple years ago we wrote about danah boyd’s brilliant discussion on how adults keep confusing risks and harms, when we know that in other settings you teach kids to understand risks in order to avoid harms. These kids seem to have internalized the same concept:

Yes, the online world has serious risks of harm. We know that. We live there. We see the harms. We live the pressures. From cyberbullying to grooming and severe mental health challenges, we want these problems fixed. But while an age ban might feel like a victory for politicians, it is not setting us up for success as we do not magically inherit digital literacy when we turn 15 or 16 or 18. We are not asking anyone to ignore them. We are asking governments to stop pretending that excluding us is the same thing as protecting us. 

We understand why many parents are worried. When they look at what’s happening online, they see risks of harm. But too often, they are misdiagnosing the problem. The answer is not to remove young people from online spaces altogether. The answer is to make those spaces safer based on our real experiences and perspectives. 

A blanket ban does not teach us how to make good decisions. It does not help us handle risk or build resilience. It does not teach digital literacy. It does not ensure better product design and it does not make us safer online. On the contrary, stripping social media away entirely misses a critical developmental window when teens can learn to navigate digital risks under the guidance of parents, guardians, and educators. 

We reject the idea that the best society can do for teenagers is to lock us out. 

They also have a list of recommendations, and most of it is really good. The first one is trickier than it looks, since a lot depends on what “require” and “safer” actually mean in practice, but the rest is spot on:

If governments are serious about protecting young people, then we need everyone, from policymakers to companies, to do the real work: 

  • Require safer platform design 
  • Set and consistently enforce meaningful rules
  • Build privacy and safety features that actually work for teens 
  • Fund relevant and comprehensive digital literacy in schools and make it mandatory (Digital literacy may be more important for adults, by the way!) 
  • Make online reporting systems easier, clearer, accepted, and more trustworthy
  • Foster a collaborative ecosystem of guidance between parents, teens, schools, and governments rather than relying on restrictions, and 
  • Most importantly, include teens in the decisions that shape our (digital) lives 

We are not problems to be managed. We are people to be heard. 

We deserve a digital world that is safer, yes, but also more open, more thoughtful, and more human. We deserve connection, fun, friendship, learning, and community and we deserve laws based on how our lives actually work, not on older generations’ definitions of “childhood.” 

Again, I imagine many people will dismiss this because of Snap’s involvement in publishing the letter, but there’s a tremendous amount of truth here. We should be listening to kids, not assuming adults know what’s best for them in all cases. We should recognize that outright bans are silly and counterproductive. And we should focus on actual solutions: digital literacy, and helping kids understand the risks so they can avoid the harms.

items.title: US Intelligence Chief Predicts More Tech Outages As Systems Undergo Upgrades
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Sunday that Americans should expect more technology outages as companies and government agencies modernize aging infrastructure. Speaking on CNN, Clayton said the upgrades are necessary to improve performance and cybersecurity but will inevitably cause "glitches, gaps, [and] interruptions in service." Reuters reports: A string of technology failures this month disrupted critical U.S. systems, including a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft outage that hit email services, a technical glitch that affected several major banks, and a temporary disruption to the National Security Agency's network.
 
Speaking on the ABC program "This Week," Clayton reiterated his previous statements that those outages were not the result of coordinated or state-sponsored actions, attributing them to technical upgrades. Clayton declined to discuss specifics of separate reports of cyberattacks on the FBI and Department of Agriculture, saying he expects investigators to provide answers "in due course." Clayton told CNN: "The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road."
 
Microsoft President Brad Smith issued a similar warning on CBS News' Face the Nation: "I think we have to be prepared, frankly, for the coming months because this isn't the type of thing that just gets done in a couple of weeks ... The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now."
